$$ D^{(2m_{1},\dots,2m_{\ell})}(P,\left(V^{1},\dots,V^{2\ell}\right))=D^{(2m_{2},\dots,2m_{\ell})}\left(D^{2m_{1}}(P,\left(V^{1},V^{2}\right)),\left(D^{m_{1}}(V_{3}),\dots,D^{m_{1}}(V^{2\ell})\right)\right) $$

and Proposition 2.13 together imply that the $(2m_{1},\dots,2m_{\ell})$ -hyperbolicity of each $\ell$ -piece is equivalent to $(2m_{2},\dots,2m_{\ell})$ -hyperbolicity of pieces corresponding with a separating starburst $D^{2m_{1}}(\mathbf{S})$ in the $(\ell-2)$ -piece $\left(D^{2m_{1}}(M),(D^{m_{1}}(V_{3}),\dots,D^{m_{1}}(V^{2(\ell-1)}))\right)$ . Our inductive hypothesis then implies that $\left(D^{2m_{1}}(M),(D^{m_{1}}(V_{3}),\dots,D^{m_{1}}(V^{2\ell})\right)$ is $(2m_{2},\dots,2m_{\ell})$ -hyperbolic, or equivalently, that $(M,(V^{1},\dots,V^{2\ell}))$ is $\mathbf{m}$ -hyperbolic.

A similar argument yields volume bounds:

$$ \displaystyle 2m_{1}\cdot\operatorname{vol}^{(2m_{1},\dots,2m_{\ell-1})}(M,\left(V^{j}\right)_{j=1}^{2(\ell-1)}) \displaystyle=\operatorname{vol}^{(2m_{2},\dots,2m_{\ell-1})}\left(D^{2m_{1}}(M,\left(V^{1},V^{2}\right)),\left(V^{j}\right)_{j=3}^{2(\ell-1)}\right) \displaystyle\geq\sum_{i}\operatorname{vol}^{(2m_{2},\dots,2m_{\ell})}\left(D^{2m_{1}}(M_{i},\left(V_{i}^{1},V_{i}^{2}\right)),\left(D^{m_{1}}(V_{i}^{j})\right)_{j=3}^{2\ell}\right) \displaystyle=2m_{1}\cdot\sum_{i}\operatorname{vol}^{(2m_{1},\dots,2m_{\ell})}(M_{i},\left(V_{i}^{j}\right)_{j=1}^{2\ell})). $$

In fact, this equality is attained if and only if equality is attained in the middle inequality above. By the inductive hypothesis, this is true if and only if each doubled surface in $\mathbf{S}$ is totally geodesic in $D^{2m_{1}}(M,(V^{1},V^{2}))$ . This is true if and only if each surface in $\mathbf{S}$ is totally geodesic in $M$ , as desired. ∎

## 3. The main theorem in the general case

### 3.1. Definitions

In Section 2, we defined suitable collections of surfaces, called $m$ -sheeted separating starbursts, which separate a 3-manifold $M$ into a disjoint union of $2m$ pieces such that hyperbolicity of the pieces implies hyperbolicity of $M$ . In fact, we may summarize this with one datum rather than $2m$ : defining the disjoint union of $\ell$ -pieces by

$$ (P,(V^{j}))\sqcup(P^{\prime},(V^{\prime j})):=(P\sqcup P^{\prime},(V^{j}\sqcup V^{\prime j})). $$

For any $\mathbf{m}\in 2\mathbb{Z}^{\ell}_{>0}$ , there is a diffeomorphism

$$ D^{\mathbf{m}}\left((P,(V^{j}))\sqcup(P^{\prime},(V^{\prime}_{j}))\right)\simeq D^{\mathbf{m}}\left(P,(V^{j})\right)\sqcup D^{\mathbf{m}}\left(P^{\prime},(V^{j})\right). $$

In particular, since we have $(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S},(V^{1},V^{2}))=\coprod_{i=1}^{2m}(M_{i},(V_{i}^{1},V_{i}^{2}))$ as in Construction 3.3, we may summarize Theorem 2.4 by stating that $2m$ -hyperbolicity of $(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S},(V^{1},V^{2}))$ implies hyperbolicity of $M$ , with volume satisfying

$$ \operatorname{vol}(M)\geq\operatorname{vol}^{2m}(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}). $$

In the case of a starburst in an $(\ell-1)$ -piece, we further have that $(2m_{1},\dots,2m_{\ell})$ -hyperbolicity of the $\ell$ -piece $\left(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S},(V^{j})_{i=1}^{2\ell}\right)$ implies $(2m_{1},\dots,2m_{\ell-1})$ -hyperbolicity of $\left(M,(V^{j})_{i1}^{2(\ell-1)}\right)$ , with volumes satisfying

$$ \operatorname{vol}^{(2m_{1},\dots,2m_{\ell-1})}\left(M\right)\geq\operatorname{vol}^{(2m_{1},\dots,2m_{\ell})}\left(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}\right). $$

This formulation is suggestive; the contruction of $(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S},(V^{j}))$ doesn’t appear to depend on the fact that $M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}$ separates into $M_{i}$ in an essential way. To expand on this, we make the following definition, which relaxes orientability of $M$ and the separation of $M$ into a cycle of pieces.

#### Definition 3.1.

Let $M$ be a 3-manifold and let $\mathbf{S}=\left\{\Sigma_{1},\dots,\Sigma_{m}\right\}$ be a set of properly embedded two-sided surfaces in $M$ . Let $E:=\bigcup_{i\neq j}\Sigma_{i}\cap\Sigma_{j}$ be the locus at which at least two surfaces intersect, and suppose that $E=\Sigma_{i}\cap\Sigma_{j}$ for each $i\neq j$ . Let $\rho:\bigcup_{i}\Sigma_{i}\backslash\backslash E\rightarrow\left\{+,-\right\}$ be a “two-coloration” of the connected components of $\Sigma_{i}\backslash\backslash E$ for each $i$ . We say that the data $(M,\mathbf{S},\rho)$ constitute an n-sheeted starburst in $M$ (often, simply a starburst) if the following conditions are met:

- (1) the intersection locus $E$ is a compact one-manifold (possibly disconnected and possibly with boundary) properly embedded in $M$ ;

- (2) there is a neighborhood $E\subset U\subset M$ and a diffeomorphism of pairs $(U,U\cap\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}\Sigma_{i}\right))\simeq(D\times E,\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}L_{i}\times E)$ which restricts to a diffeomorphism $\Sigma_{i}\cap U\simeq L_{i}\times E$ for each $i$ , with notation defined in Figure 10 and 12;

- (3) any two connected components of $\Sigma_{i}\backslash\backslash E$ who neighbor the same points of $E$ in $M$ have opposing colorations via $\rho$ ;

- (4) for each connected component of $E$ , given the induced orientations of normal bundles and labels of the lines $L_{i}\subset S_{m}$ , all orientations of normal bundles on a $+$ -labelled component of $L_{i}\setminus E$ share a direction (either clockwise or counterclockwise).

#### Remark 3.2.

We may formally define ”all $+$ -labelled components of $L_{i}\setminus E$ share direction” several equivalent ways; one convenient one is to note that the subspace of points $d(\mathbf{L})$ of $\partial(D\backslash\backslash\bigcup_{i}L_{i})$ corresponding with $\bigcup_{i}L_{i}$ have $2n$ connected components, and each surface together with an orientation of its normal bundle determines two connected components of $d(\mathbf{L})$ having either positive orientation and $+$ label or negative orientation and $-$ label, as in Construction 3.3. One may replace condition (4) with the requirement that this correspondence identifies all $2n$ components of $d(\mathbf{L})$ , or equivalently, than no $+$ and $-$ labelled components of half-lines identify the same component.

*Figure 12. Continuation of Figure 10, now using the orientation and labelling data. Part (c) includes arrows denoting the orientation, and labels denoting $\rho$ . Part (d) shows the parts of surfaces near $E$ comprising $V^{1}_{i}$ .*

For this paragraph, let $(M,\mathbf{S})$ be a separating starburst. Then, by definition, $(M,\mathbf{S})$ satisfies the first two conditions for a starburst. The portion $d(\Sigma_{i})\setminus d(E)\subset\partial M$ corresponding with $\Sigma_{i}$ can be expressed as the union of $V^{1}_{i}$ , $V^{2}_{i-1}$ , $V^{1}_{i+n}$ , and $V^{2}_{i+n-1}$ , with the first pair and last pair of surfaces corresponding with a common component of $\Sigma_{i}\backslash\backslash E$ . The parts $V^{2}_{i}$ all point clockwise local to $E$ , so we may choose the labeling $\rho|_{\Sigma_{i}}:\Sigma_{i}\backslash\backslash E\rightarrow\left\{+,-\right\}$ so that all of $V^{2}_{i}$ corresponds with either positive orientation and $+$ -labelling or negative orientation and $-$ -labelling; we may further choose labelling so that $V^{1}_{i}$ corresponds with either positive orientation and $-$ -labeling or negative orientation and $+$ -labelling. Conditions (3) and (4) then follow from the fact that $\mathbf{S}$ separates $M$ into $M_{i}$ . Hence separating starbursts are themselves starbursts, and we may reverse-engineer the notion of clockwise or clockwise side from orientations and labelling. We will use this to extend the piece structure from separating starbursts to all starbursts.

Henceforth let $(M,\mathbf{S})$ be an $m$ -sheeted starburst. We now explicitly construct surfaces rendering $M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}$ to be a piece, generalizing the piece structure on each $M_{i}$ in the separating case. In the same sense that the outer boundary of the saucer containing a tangle is separated by copies of $E$ into a clockwise and counterclockwise side, we define the piece structure by using the 2-coloration and orientation of the normal bundles of $\Sigma_{i}$ to choose surfaces which, local to the points corresponding with $E$ , appear to distinguish the clockwise and counterclockwise side as well.

#### Construction 3.3.

For $\Sigma_{i}\in\mathbf{S}$ , let $d(\Sigma_{i})$ be the union of the points in $\partial(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S})$ which correspond with $\Sigma_{i}$ , and let $d(\mathbf{S})$ be the union of the $d(\Sigma_{i})$ . Let $d(E)$ be defined similarly for $E$ .

Every point of $d(\Sigma_{i})\setminus d(E)$ corresponds with a point in $\Sigma_{i}\setminus E$ and for a point in $\Sigma_{i}\setminus E$ , there are two points in $d(\Sigma_{i})\setminus d(E)$ which correspond to it. One comes about as a boundary point on the positively oriented side of a normal bundle on $\Sigma_{i}$ and one comes about from the negatively oriented side, so we may accordingly call a point in $d(\Sigma_{i})\setminus d(E)$ positive or negative. By nature of the orientation, if two points in $d(\Sigma_{i})\setminus d(E)$ reside in the same connected component, they must either both be positive or both be negative. Hence we may refer to a positively-oriented component of $d(\Sigma_{i})\setminus d(E)$ as one whose points are positive away from $d(E)$ , and a negatively-oriented component otherwise.

Similarly, every component of $d(\Sigma)\setminus d(E)$ has points corresponding with a unique component of $\Sigma_{i}\backslash\backslash E$ , so there is a two-coloration $\bigcup_{i}d(\Sigma_{i})\setminus d(E)\rightarrow\left\{+,-\right\}$ induced by $\rho$ , and we will also call this $\rho$ . We say that a component of $d(\mathbf{S})\setminus d(E)$ (that is, a component of some $d(\Sigma_{i})\setminus d(E)$ ) as counter-clockwise-pointing if it is either $+$ -labeled and positively-oriented or $-$ -labelled and negatively-oriented, and clockwise-pointing otherwise. Let $V_{i}^{2}$ be the union of $E$ and the clockwise-pointing components of $d(\Sigma_{i})\setminus d(E)$ , and let $V_{i}^{1}$ be the union of $E$ and the counterclockwise-pointing components of $d(\Sigma_{i})\setminus d(E)$ . Let $V^{j}:=\bigcup_{i}V_{i}^{j}$ be the union of the clockwise-pointing or counterclockwise-pointing components. We visualize this via Figure 12.

By condition (4), each component of $d(E)$ separates a clockwise-pointing component and a counterclockwise-pointing component; hence $V^{1}\cap V^{2}=d(E)=\bigsqcup_{i=1}^{2m}E$ , which is a 1-manifold.

#### Remark 3.4.

In the case that every connected component of $\Sigma_{i}$ intersects $E$ , note that every allowable choice of orientations of normal bundles and labellings identifies the same piece structure on $M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}$ ; in general, varying orientations and labellings allows one to construct up to $2^{C}$ many isomorphism classes of piece structures, where $C$ is the number of connected components of $\bigcup_{i}\Sigma_{i}$ not intersecting $E$ .

This construction yields a piece structure $(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S},(V^{1},V^{2}))$ . Hence there is a notion of replication and $2m$ -hyperbolicity of a starburst, and we may ask whether generalizations of Theorem 2.4 applies in this case. But we would like to allow the intersection set $E$ of the surfaces to intersect the boundary of the manifold. This is the topic of the next subsection.

### 3.2. Boundary compatibility and the torus boundary case

In Theorem 2.4, we assumed that the manifold $M$ had only torus boundary and $E$ did not intersect the boundary. We shortly generalize these conditions. In the case that $E$ intersects a torus boundary of $M$ , let $G$ be the graph on $T$ formed by the intersection of $\bigcup_{i}\partial\Sigma_{i}$ with $T$ . We prove the following result.

#### Lemma 3.5.

If $(M,\mathbf{S})$ is an $m$ -sheeted separating starburst, $E$ intersects a torus boundary $T$ of $M$ , and the $2m$ -replicants of the corresponding pieces are all hyperbolic, then $G$ is connected, $m$ = 2, and all of the complementary regions to $G$ on $T$ are squares.

#### Proof.

Note that every surface $\Sigma_{i}$ must touch every vertex of the graph. Also, hyperbolicity of the replicants means that the replicant cannot have spherical boundaries. This would, for instance occur, if any complementary region of $G$ on $T$ is a bigon.

We first consider the simple closed curves that make up $\Sigma_{i}\cap T$ for a fixed value of $i$ . None can be trivial curves on $T$ as follows. If there were trivial curves, take an innermost such. Let $D$ be the disk it bounds on $T$ . So $D$ has no other curves from $\Sigma_{i}$ inside it. Therefore it has no vertices in its interior, since every vertex must touch a curve from $\Sigma_{i}$ . If $D$ has vertices on its boundary, there are curves from each of the other surfaces that cross it. But that there are no vertices inside $D$ implies that we can take an outermost arc from the other surfaces inside $D$ and it forms a bigon with an arc on the boundary of $D$ , which will generate a sphere in the boundary of the corresponding replicant, a contradiction to its hyperbolicity.

On the other hand, suppose there are no vertices on $\partial D$ . Then when we form $D^{2m}(M_{i})$ for the piece containing $D$ on its boundary, we again obtain a sphere boundary, contradicting hyperbolicity of the replicants.

Hence, for all $i$ , every curve in $\Sigma_{i}\cap T$ must be nontrivial on $T$ . So for each fixed $i$ , the curves in $\Sigma_{i}\cap T$ must all be parallel $(p_{i},q_{i})$ -curves. Further, the only options for complementary regions to $G$ are disks and annuli.

If there is an annulus in $M_{i}\cap T$ , take its boundary to be meridians for convenience. Then for all $i$ and all of the curves in $\Sigma_{i}\cap T$ , $q_{i}=0$ . That is to say, for all $i$ , all simple closed curves in $\Sigma_{i}\cap T$ are meridians.

Consider the first two surfaces $\Sigma_{1}$ and $\Sigma_{2}$ . The fact that all curves in their intersections with $T$ are meridians implies that any two that cross must do so an even number of times. Further, for some pair of curves $\gamma_{1}$ in $\partial\Sigma_{1}$ and $\gamma_{2}$ in $\partial\Sigma_{2}$ , there must be an arc $\alpha_{1}$ on $\gamma_{1}$ and an arc $\alpha_{2}$ on $\gamma_{2}$ such that they form a bigon with sides that are not crossed by any other curve from $\partial\Sigma_{1}$ or $\partial\Sigma_{2}$ . Additional arcs from other surfaces could enter the bigon through one of the vertices. But since there can be no vertices inside the bigon as there are no curves from $\partial\Sigma_{1}$ or $\partial\Sigma_{2}$ inside it, any such arc must just exit out the opposite vertex. Thus, they decompose the bigon into thinner bigons, which again lift to spheres in the corresponding replicants, contradicting their hyperbolicity. So there are no annuli.

We now show that $(p_{i},q_{i})\neq(p_{j},q_{j})$ for $i\neq j$ . The proof is the same argument as above. Namely if curves from $\partial\Sigma_{1}$ and $\partial\Sigma_{2}$ on $T$ are parallel, they must cross, and then we can find an innermost bigon between the two types of curves and there can be no other boundary curves of $\Sigma_{1}$ or $\Sigma_{2}$ inside the bigon formed. So only curves from one vertex to the other can appear in the bigon, which makes a thinner bigon, a contradiction.

So now if we consider a $(p_{1},q_{1})$ -curve $\gamma_{1}$ and a $(p_{2},q_{2})$ -curve $\gamma_{2}$ from two different surfaces, they must cross. But in fact they must cross a minimal amount of times, namely $|p_{1}q_{2}-p_{2}q_{1}|$ times, as if not, there will be a bigon formed between them with no other curves from these two surfaces in the bigon and the same argument shows there is a bigon.

So we have collections of parallel curves for each surface. We can always choose one set of them to be thought of as meridians. Then if there are only two surfaces, they decompose the torus into squares and $m=2$ . Then all replicants have torus boundaries corresponding to $T$ .

If there are three surfaces, the first two surface boundaries decompose the torus into squares. The third surface boundaries must intersect the first two only at their intersections. Since they cannot generate bigons, they must cut diagonally across the squares.

Note that if there were a fourth surface, it would also have to have its boundary curves on $T$ intersecting only at the existing vertices and this would force bigons. Thus, $m=2$ or 3.

In the case $m=3$ , the torus is decomposed into triangles by the graph $G$ . However, there can be no odd cycles in $G$ . This is because the cyclic order of pieces around a vertex must be preserved. Hence, for any edge in $G$ , the cyclic orders must be clockwise around one and counterclockwise around the other. In particular, this means $G$ must be a bipartite graph, with all even-length cycles. ∎

In particular, this lemma ensures that if $E$ intersects a torus boundary of $M$ , then if the replicants are hyperbolic, as we assume in Theorem 2.4, the boundaries of the replicants of the corresponding pieces are also tori.

We would like to generalize Theorems 2.4 and 2.14 to manifolds with higher genus boundary. Such a manifold is said to be tg-hyperbolic if when all torus boundaries are removed, it has a hyperbolic metric such that its higher genus boundaries are totally geodesic. This is equivalent to the fact that if the manifold is doubled across its higher genus boundaries, and the torus boundaries are again removed, the resulting manifold is hyperbolic. A tg-hyperbolic manifold has a well-defined finite hyperbolic volume.

But in order to generalize to this situation, in the case that $E$ intersects the higher genus boundary components, we need to know that the $2m$ -replicants of the corresponding pieces that intersect those boundaries also have corresponding genus greater than 1. Hence we have the following definition.

#### Definition 3.6.

Any connected sub-surface $Q_{i}$ of the boundary of $M_{i}$ that lies in the boundary of $M$ will correspond to boundary-components of $D^{2m}(M_{i},(V^{1}_{i},V^{2}_{i}))$ . We define a piece $(M_{i},(V^{1}_{i},V^{2}_{i}))$ to be boundary-compatible with the manifold $M$ from which it comes if for any connected components of $\partial M_{i}\subset\partial M$ , the corresponding boundary components of $D^{2m}(M_{i},(V^{1}_{i},V^{2}_{i}))$ have genus one if and only if the corresponding boundary components of $M$ have genus one. Note that all of the boundary-components of $D^{2m}(M_{i},(V^{1}_{i},V^{2}_{i}))$ coming from a particular connected component $Q_{i}$ of $\partial M_{i}$ will have the same genus.

### 3.3. Statement of the General Theorems

We are now ready to state the generalization of Theorem 2.4. We prove the following.

#### Theorem 3.7.

Suppose $(M,\mathbf{S},\rho)$ is an $m$ -sheeted starburst in a 3-manifold $M$ , and $(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S},(V^{1},V^{2}))$ is the associated piece. If $(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S},(V^{1},V^{2}))$ are $2m$ -hyperbolic and boundary-compatible with $M$ , then $M$ is hyperbolic, with volume satisfying

$$ \operatorname{vol}(M)\geq\operatorname{vol}^{2m}(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}). $$

Equality is attained if and only if each surface $\Sigma_{i}\subset M$ is totally geodesic.

Note that Lemma 3.5 implies that if $m>2$ , it must be the case that $E$ intersects only higher genus components of $\partial M$ to obtain hyperbolicity of the pieces.

Similarly to the separating case, a starburst in an $(\ell-1)$ -piece $(M,(V^{j})_{i=1}^{2(\ell-1)})$ yields an $\ell$ -piece $(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S},(V^{j})_{i=1}^{2\ell})$ , and there is an associated notion of $\mathbf{m}$ -hyperbolicity. We will prove the following generalization of Theorem 2.14 in this case.

#### Theorem 3.8.

Suppose that $\left(M,\left(V^{j}\right)_{j=1}^{2(\ell-1)}\right)$ is an $(\ell-1)$ -piece, suppose $(M,\mathbf{S},\rho)$ is an $m$ -sheeted, boundary-compatible starburst, and suppose the associated $\ell$ -piece $(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S},\left(V^{j}\right)_{j=1}^{2\ell})$ is $(2m_{1},\dots,2m_{\ell})$ -hyperbolic. Then, $(M,\left(V^{j}\right)_{j=1}^{2(\ell-1)})$ is $(2m_{1},\dots,2m_{\ell-1})$ -hyperbolic with volume satisfying

$$ \operatorname{vol}^{(2m_{1},\dots,2m_{\ell-1})}\left(M\right)\geq\operatorname{vol}^{(2m_{1},\dots,2m_{\ell})}\left(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}\right). $$

This equality is attained if and only if each $\Sigma\in\mathbf{S}$ is totally geodesic in $M$ .

In Subsection 3.4, we reduce Theorem 3.7 to the case that $M$ is orientable. Subsection 3.4 can be skipped by the reader only interested in working with orientable 3-manifolds.

Then, in Subsection 3.5 we give an alternative proof of Theorem 2.4 which directly uses the piece structure on $M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}$ , rather than individual $M_{i}$ . We use this as motivation to prove Theorems 3.7 and 3.8 in Subsection 3.6.

### 3.4. Reduction of Theorem 3.7 to the orientable case

In general, we denote the orientable double cover of $M$ as $M^{*}$ , with map $\pi_{M}:M^{*}\rightarrow M$ . In the case $M$ is already orientable, $M^{*}$ represents the double cover obtained by taking two copies of $M$ .

#### Proposition 3.9.

Suppose $(M,\mathbf{S})$ is an $m$ -sheeted starburst.

- (1) Let $\Sigma_{i}^{*}:=\pi_{M}^{-1}(\Sigma_{i})$ , let $E^{*}:=\pi_{M}^{-1}(E)$ , and let $\mathbf{S}^{*}:=\left\{\Sigma^{*}_{i}\right\}$ . Define labels $\rho^{*}:\bigcup_{i}\Sigma^{*}_{i}\backslash\backslash E^{*}\rightarrow\left\{+,-\right\}$ by the composition

$$ \bigcup_{i}\Sigma^{*}_{i}\backslash\backslash E^{*}\xrightarrow{\pi}\bigcup_{i}\Sigma_{i}\backslash\backslash E\xrightarrow{\rho}\left\{+,-\right\}. $$

Then, $(M^{*},\mathbf{S}^{*},\left\{\rho^{*}\right\})$ constitute an $m$ -sheeted starburst.

- (2) Cutting and $2m$ -replication commute with taking the orientable double cover; in particular, letting $(M^{*}\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}^{*},(V^{1*},V^{2*}))$ be the piece on the orientable double cover, we have

$$ D^{2m}(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S},(V^{1},V^{2}))^{*}=D^{2m}(M^{*}\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}^{*},(V^{1*},V^{2*})). $$

For part (1), our argument will extend naturally to say that, for an $m$ -sheeted starburst $(M,\mathbf{S},\left\{\rho\right\})$ and a finite covering map $\pi:M^{\prime}\rightarrow M$ , the set of preimages $\pi^{-1}(\mathbf{S}):=\left\{\pi^{-1}(\Sigma_{i})\mid\Sigma_{i}\in\mathbf{S}\right\}$ endowed with labels given by composition

$$ {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho\pi:\bigcup_{i}\pi^{-1}(\Sigma_{i})\backslash\backslash\pi^{-1}(E)} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\bigcup_{i}\Sigma_{i}\backslash\backslash E} {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\left\{+,-\right\}} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi} \scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho} $$

constitute an $m$ -sheeted starburst in $M^{\prime}$ . Verifying this will consist mostly of noting that each condition in Definition 3.1 can be verified locally, sometimes verifying compatibility of local data between certain pairs of points.

#### Proof of Proposition 3.9.

Part (1). Each $\Sigma_{i}^{*}$ is a properly embedded surface in $M^{*}$ . A trivialization of the normal bundle of $\Sigma_{i}$ lifts to a trivialization of the normal bundle of $\Sigma_{i}^{*}$ , so each $\Sigma_{i}^{*}$ is a two-sided surface.

The intersection locus $E^{*}=\bigcup_{i\neq j}\Sigma_{i}^{*}\cap\Sigma_{j}^{*}$ satisfies $E^{*}=\pi^{-1}(\Sigma_{i}\cap\Sigma_{j})=\Sigma_{i}^{*}\cap\Sigma_{j}^{*}$ for any $i\neq j$ . Furthermore, $E^{*}$ is the preimage of a 1-manifold $E$ under a covering map, so it is a 1-manifold.

The existence of a diffeomorphism $(U,U\cap(\bigcup_{i}\Sigma_{i}))\simeq(D\times E,S_{m}\times E)$ respecting the cyclic order is equivalent to existence, for each point $p\in E$ , of a neighborhood $U_{p}$ of $p$ and a diffeomorphism $(U_{p},U_{p}\cap(\bigcup_{i}\Sigma_{i}))\simeq(D\times I,S_{m}\times I)$ respecting the cyclic order of $\mathbf{S}$ and $S_{m}$ for each $p$ . For each $p^{*}\in E^{*}$ , composing with a local diffeomorphism $U_{p^{*}}\xrightarrow{\sim}\pi U_{p^{*}}$ of a neighborhood $U_{p^{*}}$ of $p^{*}$ yields such a diffeomorphism.

Similarly, compatibility of the direction induced by orientations of the normal bundles of $\Sigma_{i}$ and by $\rho$ can be verified local to each point of $E$ ; since the orientation and labeling are compatible with a local diffeomorphism $\pi$ , this compatibility on $(M^{*},\mathbf{S}^{*},\left\{\rho^{*}\right\})$ follows from compatibility on $(M,\mathbf{S},\left\{\rho^{*}\right\})$ . Hence we have defined an $m$ -sheeted starburst in $M^{*}$ .

Part (2). We may characterize the cover $(M^{*}\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}^{*})\rightarrow M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}$ on an open set $(M^{*}\setminus\mathbf{S}^{*})\rightarrow M\setminus\mathbf{S}$ . The latter is the restriction of the orientable double cover of $M$ onto an open set, and hence an immersed submanifold of codimension 0. Hence it is the orientable double cover, and we have $(M^{*}\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}^{*})\simeq(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S})^{*}$ .

The orientable double cover is compatible with disjoint unions, so the induced cover on $\coprod_{i=1}^{2m}(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S})$ is the orientable double cover. The covering translations permute fibers, and the surfaces $V^{j*}$ are given by the preimages of $V^{j*}$ , with the identifications defining $D^{2m}(M^{*}\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}^{*},(V^{1*},V^{2*}))$ defined fiberwise; hence the orientable double cover on $\coprod_{i=1}^{2m}(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S})$ descends to the orientable double cover on $D^{2m}(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S},(V^{1*},V^{2*}))$ , i.e. the cover $D^{2m}(M^{*}\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}^{*},(V^{1*},V^{2*}))\rightarrow D^{2m}(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S},(V^{1},V^{2}))$ is isomorphic to the orientable double cover, and in particular we have an diffeomorphism of their total spaces, as we wanted to show. ∎

By this proposition, we are able to reduce to the orientable case by passing to the orientable double cover. Hyperbolicity of $D^{2m}(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S},(V^{1},V^{2}))$ implies hyperbolicity of $D^{2m}(M^{*}\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}^{*},(V^{1*},V^{2*}))$ , which implies hyperbolicity of $M^{*}$ , which implies hyperbolicity of $M$ . Additionally, we have

$$ \operatorname{vol}(M)=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{vol}(M^{*})\geq\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{vol}^{2m}(M^{*}\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}^{*},(V^{1*},V^{2*}))=\operatorname{vol}^{2m}(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S},(V^{1},V^{2})). $$

with equality attained if and only if each element of $\mathbf{S}^{*}$ is totally geodesic in $M^{*}$ , which occurs if and only if each element of $\mathbf{S}$ is totally geodesic in $M$ .

### 3.5. A second proof of Theorem 2.4 (the main theorem for a separating starburst)

For the duration of this subsection and Subsection 3.6 we fix the notation $\mathbf{m}=(2m_{1},\dots,2m_{\ell})$ , $(M,\mathbf{S})$ , and $(V^{j})_{i=1}^{2\ell}$ as in Theorem 3.7, and we assume that $\left(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S},(V^{j})_{i=1}^{2\ell}\right)$ is $\mathbf{m}$ -hyperbolic.

This subsection focuses mainly on giving an analog of the proof given for Theorem 2.4 without constructions that essentially rely on the separating condition. This will provide motivation for the proof of Theorem 3.7 in Subsection 3.6. However, the proof of Theorem 3.7 is independent of this subsection.

Recall the set $W$ of cyclic words on alphabet $\left\{T_{i}\right\}$ parameterizing the bracelet links formed by the tangles $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ of a generic bracelet link on $2m$ tangles, as defined in Construction 2.6. We had previously defined a set of manifolds $\left\{\mathcal{S}(w)\mid w\in W\right\}$ as the topological foundation of our strategy.

However, the manifold $\mathcal{S}(w)$ consisted of individual pieces $M_{i}$ , and hence it cannot directly generalize to $M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}$ . Intuitively, we need to fill in the remaining $(M_{j})_{i\neq j}$ corresponding with each copy of $M_{i}$ in $\mathcal{S}(w)$ ; in the separating case, this can be done simply by defining the manifolds

$$ \widetilde{\mathcal{S}}\left(T_{i_{1}}\cdots T_{i_{2m}}\right):=\coprod_{j=1}^{2m}\mathcal{S}\left(T_{i_{1}+j}\cdots T_{i_{2m}+j}\right) $$

and extending this to $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}[W]$ by $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(\sum_{i}w_{i}):=\coprod_{i}\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(w_{i})$ .

Our manifolds are grounded to $M$ and $D^{2m}(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S},(V^{1},V^{2}))$ by the following identifications:

$$ \displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}\left(T_{1}\cdots T_{2m}\right) \displaystyle=2m\cdot\mathcal{S}\left(T_{1}\cdots T_{2m}\right) \displaystyle=\coprod_{i=1}^{2m}M \displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(T_{1}^{2m}) \displaystyle=\coprod_{i=1}^{2m}\mathcal{S}(T_{i}^{2m}) \displaystyle=\coprod_{i=1}^{2m}D^{2m}(M_{i},(V^{1}_{i},V^{2}_{i})) \displaystyle=D^{2m}(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S},(V^{1},V^{2})). $$

Furthermore, there is a natural notion of volume

$$ \widetilde{\operatorname{vol}}(w):=\operatorname{vol}\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(w) $$

with the volume of non-hyperbolic manifolds equal to 0. It suffices to prove that $\widetilde{\operatorname{vol}}\left(T_{1}\cdots T_{2m}\right)\geq\widetilde{\operatorname{vol}}\left(T_{1}^{2m}\right)$ .

In fact, the relation

$$ 2\widetilde{\operatorname{vol}}(a_{1}a_{2})\geq\widetilde{\operatorname{vol}}(a_{1}a_{1}^{R})+\widetilde{\operatorname{vol}}(a_{2}a_{2}^{R}) $$

follows from the same relation for the volume of each summand in (8). This together with the algebra of Subsection 2.2 immediately imply Theorem 2.4.

### 3.6. Proof of the main theorem in the general case

Using the results of Subsection 3.4, we henceforth assume that $M$ is orientable. By boundary compatibility, we may double across higher genus boundary, which takes the original starburst to another starburst in the resulting manifold, and henceforth assume that $M$ has torus boundary.

As exemplified in Subsection 3.5, we may prove Theorem 3.7 via the following strategy:

- (1) First, we define a set of manifolds $\left\{\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(w)\mid w\in W\right\}$ such that $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(T_{i}^{2m})=D^{2m}(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S},(V^{1},V^{2}))$ and $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(T_{1}\cdots T_{2m})$ is the total space of a $2m$ -fold cover of $M$ .

- (2) Next, we prove the relation $2\operatorname{vol}\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(a_{1}a_{2})\geq\operatorname{vol}\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(a_{1}a_{1}^{R})+\operatorname{vol}\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(a_{2}a_{2}^{R})$ holds in this case.

- (3) Last, we use the algebraic results given in Subsection 2.2 to prove the theorem.

We recall some notation for the purpose of defining $\widetilde{S}(w)$ . Recall that the set $d(\Sigma_{i})\subset\partial M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}$ consists of the points corresponding with $\Sigma_{i}$ ; for each $i$ we write $V_{i}^{2}$ for the clockwise side of the points of $d(\Sigma_{i})$ and $V^{i}_{1}$ for the counter-clockwise side of the points of $d(\Sigma_{i+1})$ . We have $V^{j}=\bigsqcup_{i}V^{j}_{i}.$

In this language, we can describe the $2m$ -replicant as

$$ D^{2m}(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S},(V^{1},V^{2}))=\frac{\coprod_{k=1}^{2m}(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S})}{\left(V_{i}^{1},2k\right)\sim\left(V_{i}^{2},2k+1\right)\hskip 10.0pt\text{and}\hskip 10.0pt\left(V_{i}^{2},2k-1\right)\sim\left(V_{i}^{1},2k\right)} $$

We will extend this to arbitrary elements of $\widetilde{W}$ in the following construction.

#### Construction 3.10.

Setting $\tilde{w}=t_{1}\cdots t_{2m}$ , and fixing (arbitrarily) a choice of first letter, define

$$ \displaystyle R^{1}(k,\tilde{w}) \displaystyle:=\begin{cases}1&\text{if}\hskip 2.84544ptt_{k}=T_{j}\text{ for some }j\\
2&\text{if}\hskip 2.84544ptt_{k}=T_{j}^{R}\text{ for some }j\\
\end{cases} \displaystyle R^{2}(k,\tilde{w}) \displaystyle:=\begin{cases}2&\text{if}\hskip 2.84544ptt_{k}=T_{j}\text{ for some }j\\
1&\text{if}\hskip 2.84544ptt_{k}=T_{j}^{R}\text{ for some }j\\
\end{cases} \displaystyle\text{if}\hskip 10.0ptt_{k}\in\left\{T_{j},T_{j}^{R}\right\}\hskip 10.0pt\text{and}\hskip 10.0ptt_{k+1}\in\left\{T_{j^{\prime}},T_{j^{\prime}}^{R}\right\}\hskip 60.0pt\Delta(k,\tilde{w}) \displaystyle:=j^{\prime}-j $$

Using this language, we may define the following:

$$ \widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(\tilde{w}):=\frac{\coprod_{k=1}^{2m}(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S})}{\left(V_{i}^{R^{1}(2k,\tilde{w})},2k\right)\sim\left(V_{i+\Delta(2k,\tilde{w})}^{R^{2}(2k+1,\tilde{w})},2k+1\right)\hskip 10.0pt\text{and}\hskip 10.0pt\left(V_{i}^{R^{2}(2k-1,\tilde{w})},2k-1\right)\sim\left(V_{i+\Delta(2k-1,\tilde{w})}^{R^{1}(2k,\tilde{w})},2k\right)} $$

Note that there exists a diffeomorphism $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(T_{1}T_{2})\simeq\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(T_{1}^{R}T_{2}^{R})$ , and hence this descends to a construction of a $W$ -indexed collection of manifolds.

This generalizes the construction of $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(w)$ in the separating case; for instance, in that case the identification

$$ \left(V_{i}^{R_{1}(2k,w)},2k\right)\sim\left(V_{i+\Delta(2k,w)}^{R_{2}(2k+1,w)},2k+1\right) $$

represents the gluing of the piece at index $2k$ to the piece at index $2k+1$ within the submanifold $\mathcal{S}(t_{j_{1}+i}\cdots t_{j_{2m}+i})\subset\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(w)$ . The reader may verify that, for each tuple $(i,j,k)$ , there is a unique tuple $(i^{\prime},j^{\prime},k^{\prime})$ such that there exists an identification $(V_{i}^{j},k)\sim(V_{i^{\prime}}^{j^{\prime}},k^{\prime})$ in $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(w)$ .

Now that we’ve defined $\widetilde{S}(w)$ , we verify its relationship with $(M,\mathbf{S})$ in the following lemma.

#### Lemma 3.11.

Let $(M,\mathbf{S},\left\{\rho\right\})$ be an $m$ -sheeted starburst, and let $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(w)$ be the corresponding word for each $w\in W$ .

- (1) For each $j$ there is a diffeomorphism

$$ \widetilde{\mathcal{S}}\left(T_{j}^{2m}\right)\simeq D^{2m}(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}) $$

so that $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}\left(T_{j}^{2m}\right)$ is hyperbolic if and only if $M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}$ is $2m$ -hyperbolic, in which case we have

$$ \widetilde{\operatorname{vol}}\left(T_{j}^{2m}\right)=2m\cdot\operatorname{vol}^{2m}(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}). $$

- (2) There is a $2m$ -fold covering map

$$ \widetilde{\mathcal{S}}\left(T_{1}\cdots T_{2m}\right)\rightarrow M $$

so that $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}\left(T_{1}\cdots T_{2m}\right)$ is hyperbolic if and only if $M$ is hyperbolic, in which case we have

$$ \widetilde{\operatorname{vol}}\left(T_{1}\cdots T_{2m}\right)=2m\cdot\operatorname{vol}(M). $$

#### Proof.

Part (1) follows by noting that

$$ \widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(T_{j}^{2m})=\frac{\coprod_{k=1}^{2m}(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S})}{\left(V_{i}^{1},2k\right)\sim\left(V_{i}^{2},2k+1\right)\hskip 10.0pt\text{and}\hskip 10.0pt\left(V_{i}^{2},2k-1\right)\sim\left(V_{i}^{1},2k\right)}=D^{2m}(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S},(V^{1},V^{2})) $$

For part (2), note that

$$ \widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(T_{1}\cdots T_{2m})=\frac{\coprod_{k=1}^{2m}(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S})}{\left(V_{i}^{2},k\right)\sim\left(V^{i+1}_{1},k+1\right)} $$

has points either given by a point in the interior of $M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}$ , by an equivalence class of two points $(p,k)$ and $(p^{\prime},k^{\prime})$ where $p$ and $p^{\prime}$ are points of $V_{i}^{2}$ and $V_{i+1}^{1}$ who correspond with the same point of $\Sigma_{i+1}$ , or by an equivalence class of $2m$ points who correspond with the same point of $E$ . This correspondence outlines a map

$$ \widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(T_{1}\cdots T_{2m})\rightarrow M. $$

We will exhibit this map as a covering map, with local trivialization at points in the interior of $M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}$ by an $M$ -neighborhood which doesn’t intersect any element of $\mathbf{S}$ . For points on some $\Sigma_{i}\setminus E$ , we may choose the trivializing neighborhood to be the union of two “half-balls” in two different copies of $M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}$ in $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(T_{1}\cdots T_{2m})$ . For points on $E$ , we may choose the trivializing neighborhood to be the union of $2m$ “slices” in the $2m$ copies of $M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}$ in $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(T_{1}\cdots T_{2m})$ .

Note that the fiber of each point $p\in M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}$ is given by $\left\{(p,k)\mid 1\leq k\leq 2m\right\}$ . Hence the fibers of this covering map have size $2m$ , as desired. ∎

As outlined in our strategy, we now prove the following proposition, implementing the relations used in the proof of Theorem 2.4.

#### Lemma 3.12.

Suppose that $w=a_{1}a_{2}\in W$ where $\operatorname{len}(a_{1})=m$ , and define $w_{j}:=a_{j}a_{j}^{R}$ . If $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(w_{1})$ an $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(w_{2})$ are hyperbolic, then $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(w)$ is hyperbolic, with volume satisfying

$$ 2\widetilde{\operatorname{vol}}(w)\geq\widetilde{\operatorname{vol}}\left(w_{1}+w_{2}\right). $$

#### Proof.

Assume without loss of generality that $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(w_{1})$ was constructed fixing the first letter of $a_{1}$ as the first letter of the word. Then, there is a diffeomorphism of $\coprod_{k=1}^{2m}M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}$ sending $\left(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S},k\right)\rightarrow\left(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S},2m-k\right)$ . For a general word $v$ this descends to a diffeormophism $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(v)\rightarrow\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(v^{R})$ ; in the case of a palindromic word, this descends to a diffeomorphism of $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(v)$ .

In particular, the fixed point set of this diffeomorphism is the surface

$$ F_{j}:=\bigcup_{k}\left(V_{1}^{R_{1}(1,w)}\cup V_{m}^{R_{2}(m,w)},k\right)\subset\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(w_{j}). $$

By Theorem 1.4, $F_{j}$ is totally geodesic; since $a_{1}a_{2}\in W$ , the surfaces $F_{1}$ and $F_{2}$ are diffeomorphic. Hence we may form the 3-manifold $X$ by gluing together the $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(a_{j}a_{j}^{R})\backslash\backslash F_{j}$ along a diffeomorphism of the points corresponding to $F_{j}$ induced by the diffeomorphism $F_{1}\simeq F_{2}$ . Then, by Theorem 1.5, $X$ is hyperbolic, with volume satisfying

$$ \operatorname{vol}(X)\geq\widetilde{\operatorname{vol}}(w_{1}+w_{2}). $$

To prove the lemma, it suffices to supply a double cover $p:X\rightarrow\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(w)$ . This may be defined by noting that there exists a map $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(w_{1})\backslash\backslash F_{1}\sqcup\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(w_{2})\backslash\backslash F_{2}\rightarrow\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(w)$ identifying the points corresponding with word $a_{j}$ in the domain with the same points corresponding with $a_{j}$ in the codomain; two points in the domain are identified by the diffeomorphism of $F_{1}$ and $F_{2}$ only if they are mapped to the same point of $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(w)$ , so this descends to a map $p:X\rightarrow\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(w)$ .

We verify that $p$ is a covering map. For a point contained within the points corresponding with subword $a_{j}$ and away from the image of $F_{j}$ in $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(w)$ , we may choose a trivializing neighborhood which is contained in the points corresponding with $a_{j}$ . For a point on the image of $F_{j}$ , we may choose the neighborhood composed of the union of “half-balls” in the points corresponding with each $a_{1}$ and $a_{2}$ . Hence this is a covering map.

It is clear that this map has fibers of size 2, and hence $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(w)$ is hyperbolic with volume satisfying

$$ 2\cdot\widetilde{\operatorname{vol}}(w)=\operatorname{vol}(X)\geq\widetilde{\operatorname{vol}}(w_{1}+w_{2}), $$

as desired. ∎

#### Proof of Theorem 3.7.

Given Lemmas 3.11 and 3.12, the proof of Proposition 2.7 yields hyperbolicity of $M$ and the inequality

$$ \displaystyle 2m\cdot\operatorname{vol}(M) \displaystyle=\widetilde{\operatorname{vol}}(T_{1}\cdots T_{2m}) \displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{2m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\widetilde{\operatorname{vol}}(T_{i}) \displaystyle=2m\cdot\operatorname{vol}^{2m}(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}). $$

We now characterize when this equality is attained. Let $a_{1}:=T_{1}\cdots T_{m}$ and let $a_{2}:=T_{m+1}\cdots T_{2m}$ . Then, in the notation of Lemma 4, the image of the surfaces $F^{1}_{j}\subset\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(a_{j}a_{j}^{R})$ in $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(T_{1}\cdots T_{2m})$ is given by the preimage of $\Sigma_{1}$ under the covering map $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(T_{1}\cdots T_{2m})\rightarrow M$ . Call this surface $F^{1}$ , and note that $F^{1}$ is totally geodesic if and only if $\Sigma_{1}$ is totally geodesic; this generalizes immediately to $\Sigma_{j}$ , and let the associated surface be $F^{j}$ .

Suppose first that some $\Sigma_{j}$ is not totally geodesic. Without loss of generality, we may fix $j=1$ . Then, note that $F^{1}\subset\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(T_{1}\cdots T_{2m})$ is not totally geodesic, so its preimage in the total space of the double cover $X\rightarrow\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(T_{1}\cdots T_{2m})$ is not totally geodesic either. Then, since $X$ is formed by cutting and pasting $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(a_{j}a_{j}^{R})$ along diffeomorphisms of totally geodesic surfaces, Theorem 1.5 implies that $\operatorname{vol}(X)>\widetilde{\operatorname{vol}}(a_{1}a_{1}^{R})+\widetilde{\operatorname{vol}}(a_{2}a_{2}^{R})$ . This in turn implies

$$ \displaystyle 4m\cdot\operatorname{vol}(M) \displaystyle=2\cdot\widetilde{\operatorname{vol}}(T_{1}\cdots T_{2m}) \displaystyle=\operatorname{vol}(X) \displaystyle>\widetilde{\operatorname{vol}}(a_{1}a_{1}^{R})+\widetilde{\operatorname{vol}}(a_{2}a_{2}^{R}) \displaystyle\geq 4m\cdot\operatorname{vol}^{\cdot}(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}), $$

as desired.

Suppose conversely that each $\Sigma_{i}$ is totally geodesic; then, each of the surfaces $F^{j}\subset\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(T_{1}\cdots T_{2m})$ are totally geodesic, and hence each of the preimages of these surfaces in $X$ are totally geodesic. We may repeatedly cut along totally geodesic surfaces to yield $\coprod_{k=1}^{2m}(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S})$ , and glue along isometric totally geodesic surfaces to yield $\widetilde{\mathcal{S}}(T_{i})=D^{2m}(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S},(V^{1},V^{2}))$ , directly yielding the equality

$$ 2m\cdot\operatorname{vol}(M)=\widetilde{\operatorname{vol}}(T_{1}\cdots T_{2m})=\operatorname{vol}^{2m}(M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}). $$

∎

Having proven our theorem in the case of a starburst in a manifold, we may extend our theorem to starbursts in $\ell$ -pieces identically to our extension from Theorem 2.4 to Theorem 2.14, with references to Theorem 2.4 replaced by Theorem 3.7, and omitting the word “separating.”

### 3.7. Composition of pieces

In the following short section, we state and prove a corollary to Theorem 3.7 about combining hyperbolic pieces. We will use this to prove hyperbolicity of composition of tangles in Sections 4 and 5.

#### Corollary 3.13.

Let $\left\{(P_{i},(V_{i}^{1},V_{i}^{2}))\right\}$ be a set of $n$ pieces, each $2mn$ -hyperbolic, equipped with diffeomorphisms $\phi_{i}:V_{i}^{2}\xrightarrow{\sim}V_{i+1}^{1}$ for each $1\leq i\leq{n-1}$ . Then, the piece

$$ (P,(V_{1}^{1},V_{n}^{2}))\hskip 50.0pt\text{where}\hskip 50.0ptP=\frac{\coprod_{i}P_{i}}{V_{i}^{2}\sim_{\phi_{i}}V_{i+1}^{2}} $$

is $2m$ -hyperbolic, with volume satisfying

$$ \operatorname{vol}^{2m}(P)\geq\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{vol}^{2mn}(P_{i}). $$

#### Proof.

Note that $D^{2m}(P,(V_{1}^{1},V_{n}^{2}))$ contains, by tracking the images of $V_{i}^{j}$ , an $mn$ -sheeted starburst $\mathbf{S}$ which separates the manifold into $m$ -namy copies of $P_{i}$ for each $i$ . Hence Theorem 3.7 applied to the replicant $D^{2m}(P,(V_{1}^{1},V_{n}^{2}))$ yields that the manifold is hyperbolic, with volume bound as described in the corollary. ∎

## 4. Applications to knot theory

Given a manifold $M$ and a surface $\Sigma\subset\partial M$ , we define a tangle in $(M,\Sigma)$ to be an embedded compact 1-manifold in $M$ with boundary contained in $\Sigma$ . Given an $\ell$ -piece $(P,(V^{j}))$ , we define a tangle in $(P,(V^{j}))$ to be a tangle in $(P,\bigcup_{n}V_{2n-1}\cap V_{2n})$ .

A link may be viewed as a tangle with no arcs. Given a tangle in an $\ell$ -piece $(M,\left(V_{i}\right))$ and a starburst $(M,\mathbf{S},\rho)$ in the $\ell$ -piece, there is an associated tangle in the $(\ell+1)$ -piece on $M\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}$ . Further, if we have an $\ell$ -piece that is a disjoint union $(M\sqcup M^{\prime},\left\{V_{i}\sqcup V^{\prime}_{i}\right\})$ containing a tangle $\mathcal{T}$ , then $\mathcal{T}$ decomposes into the disjoint union of tangles in $(M,\left\{V_{i}\right\})$ and $(M^{\prime},\left\{V^{\prime}_{i}\right\})$ .

We explore various applications of Theorem 3.7 to the theory of links that are constructed out of tangles. In Subsection 4.1 we explore hyperbolic links within the thickened torus, which can be thought of as the complement of the Hopf link in $S^{3}$ . We decompose the links into thickened-cylinder tangles, and further decompose those into cubical tangles. In Subsection 4.2, we consider links in an open solid torus, which can be thought of as the complement of a trivial component in $S^{3}$ . There, we decompose links into wedge tangles. Following this, in Subsection 4.3 we explore hyperbolic links in the 3-sphere which decompose into a cycle of saucer tangles.

Later, in Theorem 5.1, we show that $2n$ -hyperbolicity of saucer tangles implies $2m$ -hyperbolicity for any $m\geq n$ , and hence a cycle of $n\geq 2m$ saucer tangles which are each $2m$ -hyperbolic glue together to yield a hyperbolic link. We decompose saucer tangles further into tetrahedral tangles, and prove the corresponding results there.

In Subsection 4.4, we consider torus lattice links in $S^{2}\times S^{1}$ and decompose them into thickened bigon tangles, proving similar results in this context as well.

### 4.1. Links within the thickened torus

Let $T:=S^{1}\times S^{1}$ be the torus. We define two different classes of tangles arising from the study of links in $T\times I$ .

#### Definition 4.1.

Let $C:=S^{1}\times I\times I$ be the thickened cylinder and let $R_{0}:=S^{1}\times I\times\left\{0\right\}$ and $R_{1}:=S^{1}\times I\times\left\{1\right\}$ be the annuli at heights $\{0\}$ and $\{1\}$ . A thickened-cylinder tangle $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ is a tangle in $(C,R_{0}\cup R_{1})$ , with endpoints in the two annuli at the ends of the thickened cylinder. By reflecting across $R_{0}$ and $R_{1}$ , a thickened-cylinder tangle $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ determines a link $D^{2}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right)\subset S^{1}\times S^{1}\times I$ in a thickened torus. We say that $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ is 2-hyperbolic if $D^{2}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right)$ is a hyperbolic link, in which case we define

$$ \operatorname{vol}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right):=\frac{\operatorname{vol}\left(D^{2}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right)\right)}{2}. $$

Let $Q=I^{3}$ be the cube. Define the top and bottom faces $R_{0i}:=I\times\left\{i\right\}\times I$ and the left and right faces $R_{1i}:=I\times I\times\left\{i\right\}$ . A cubical tangle $\mathcal{T}_{ij}$ is a tangle in $(Q,I\times\partial(I^{2})-I\times\partial I\times\partial I)$ . By reflecting in two opposite faces of the cube to obtain a second copy glued to the first, a cubical tangle $\mathcal{T}_{ij}$ determines a thickened-cylinder tangle. Via another reflection operation, this in turn determines a link $D^{(2,2)}\left(\mathcal{T}_{ij}\right)\subset S^{1}\times S^{1}\times I$ in a thickened torus. We say that $\mathcal{T}_{ij}$ is $(2,2)$ -hyperbolic if $D^{(2,2)}\left(\mathcal{T}_{ij}\right)$ is a hyperbolic link, in which case we define

$$ \operatorname{vol}^{(2,2)}\left(\mathcal{T}_{ij}\right):=\frac{\operatorname{vol}\left(D^{(2,2)}\left(\mathcal{T}_{ij}\right)\right)}{4}. $$

See Figure 13 for cubical tangle $\mathcal{T}$ that when doubled, yields a thickened-cylinder tangle, which when doubled again generates $D^{(2,2)}(\mathcal{T})$ .

*Figure 13. A cubical tangle generates a thickened-cylinder tangle which in turn generates a link in a thickened torus.*

The following theorems summarize the situations of Figures 1 and 2, and is an easy corollary of Theorem 3.7.

#### Theorem 4.2.

Let $L\subset T\times I$ be a link in a thickened torus such that there exists disjoint surfaces separating $L$ into thickened-cylinder tangles $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ and each $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ is 2-hyperbolic. Then $L$ is hyperbolic, and its volume satisfies

$$ \operatorname{vol}(L)\geq\sum_{i}\operatorname{vol}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right). $$

∎

#### Theorem 4.3.

Let $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ be a thickened-cylinder tangle, and suppose there are disjoint surfaces separating $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ into a cycle $\mathcal{T}_{ij}$ of cubical tangles and each $\mathcal{T}_{ij}$ is $(2,2)$ -hyperbolic. Then, $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ is $2$ -hyperbolic within, with volume satisfying

$$ \operatorname{vol}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right)\geq\sum_{j}\operatorname{vol}^{(2,2)}\left(\mathcal{T}_{ij}\right). $$

If a link $L$ in a thickened torus decomposes into cubical tangles such that each $\mathcal{T}_{ij}$ is $(2,2)$ -hyperbolic, then $L$ is hyperbolic with volume satisfying

$$ \operatorname{vol}(L)\geq\sum_{ij}\operatorname{vol}^{(2,2)}\left(\mathcal{T}_{ij}\right). $$

∎

Such surfaces as in Theorem 4.2 can be found by taking a sequence of disjoint punctured annuli tracing out a $(p,q)$ -curve on each boundary torus of $T\times I$ . Since there is a homeomorphism of $T\times I$ taking such a punctured annulus to one bounding meridians, Theorem 4.2 may be pictured as cutting the thickened torus along meridians as in Figure 1. Further, Theorem 4.3 may be pictured by cutting a thickened cylinder into cubes, as in Figure 2.

Note that diffeomorphisms of pieces lift to diffeomorphisms of their $2n$ -replicants. Hence Mostow-Prasad rigidity implies that we may replace any piece with a diffeomorphic piece while maintaining the same information regarding hyperbolicity and volume. Using this, we may replace each thickened-cylinder tangle with one whose endpoints are “standardized” such that whenever thickened-cylinder tangle $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ has the same number of endpoints at its top as $\mathcal{T}_{j}$ has at its bottom, there is an evident gluing of the tangles

$$ (C,\mathcal{T}_{i}\circ\mathcal{T}_{j}):=(C,\mathcal{T}_{i})\cup_{R_{1}\sim R_{0}}(C,\mathcal{T}_{j}) $$

which attaches the first copy of $R_{1}$ to the second copy of $R_{0}$ .

Through an analogous process, we may define two ways of gluing cubical tangles: top-to-bottom, or left-to-right, written

$$ (Q,\mathcal{T}_{ij}\circ_{a}\mathcal{T}_{kl}):=(Q,\mathcal{T}_{ij})\cup_{R_{a0}\sim R_{a1}}(Q,\mathcal{T}_{kl})) $$

whenever the numbers of endpoints are compatible.

The following establishes a relationship between hyperbolicity and composition, and it follows as a clear application of Theorem 3.8.

#### Proposition 4.4.

Suppose $\mathcal{T}_{i},\mathcal{T}_{j}$ are $2$ -hyperbolic thickened-cylinder tangles, and suppose that that $\mathcal{T}_{i}\circ\mathcal{T}_{j}$ is defined. Then, $\mathcal{T}_{i}\circ\mathcal{T}_{j}$ is $2$ -hyperbolic with volume satisfying

$$ \operatorname{vol}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\circ\mathcal{T}_{j}\right)\geq\operatorname{vol}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right)+\operatorname{vol}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T}_{j}\right) $$

Suppose instead that $\mathcal{T}_{ij},\mathcal{T}_{kl}$ are $(2,2)$ -hyperbolic cubical tangles and suppose that $\mathcal{T}_{ij}\circ_{a}\mathcal{T}_{kl}$ is defined. Then, $\mathcal{T}_{ij}\circ_{a}\mathcal{T}_{kl}$ is $(2,2)$ -hyperbolic in a thickened torus, with volume satisfying

$$ \operatorname{vol}^{(2,2)}\left(\mathcal{T}_{ij}\circ_{a}\mathcal{T}_{kl}\right)\geq\operatorname{vol}^{(2,2)}\left(\mathcal{T}_{ij}\right)+\operatorname{vol}^{(2,2)}\left(\mathcal{T}_{kl}\right) $$

∎

In a subsequent paper [22], we will provide many examples of 2-hyperbolic thickened-cylinder tangles.

### 4.2. Links within a solid torus

Let $V:=D\times S^{1}$ be the solid torus, where $D$ is the 2-dimensional disk. Unlike the thickened torus case, cutting links $L\subset V$ via starbursts that intersect the boundary $\partial V=T$ in meridians and longitudes yields tangles in different ambient spaces. In particular, cutting along a starburst with longitude boundaries yields a cycle of tangles living in cyclical wedges, and cutting along a surface bounded by disjoint meridians yields a cycle of tangles living in solid cylinders. Each of these may be further cut into square tangles that live in wedges.

We give analogous definitions to the thickened torus case in order to find lower bounds on volumes of links $L\subset V$ .

#### Definition 4.5.

A solid-cylinder tangle $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ is a tangle in $(D\times I,D\times\partial I)$ . In a similar manner to thickened-cylinder tangles, doubling a solid-cylinder tangle $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ over $D\times\partial I$ determines a link in a solid torus, written

$$ (V,D^{2}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right)):=(D\times I,\mathcal{T}_{i})\cup_{D\times\partial I}(D\times\mathcal{T}_{i}). $$

We say that $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ is $2$ -hyperbolic if $D^{2}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right)$ is hyperbolic, in which case we define

$$ \operatorname{vol}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right):=\frac{\operatorname{vol}\left(D^{2}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right)\right)}{2}. $$

Let $P$ be the solid triangle, and let $F\subset P$ be the union of two edges of $P$ . A cyclic wedge tangle $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ is a tangle in $(S^{1}\times P,S^{1}\times F)$ . Via the reflection $r:P\rightarrow P$ sending one edge of $F$ to another, a cyclic wedge tangle $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ determines a reflected cyclic wedge tangle $\mathcal{T}_{i}^{R}$ . Then, gluing adjacent tangles together along the length $2n$ cycle sequence $(\mathcal{T}_{i},\mathcal{T}_{i}^{R},\dots,\mathcal{T}_{i}^{R})$ determines a link $D^{2n}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right)\subset V$ , called the $2n$ -replicant. We say that $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ is $2n$ -hyperbolic if $D^{2n}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right)$ is hyperbolic, in which case we define the volume

$$ \operatorname{vol}^{2n}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right):=\frac{\operatorname{vol}\left(D^{2n}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right)\right)}{2n}. $$

A wedge tangle $\mathcal{T}_{ij}$ is a tangle in $(I\times P,I\times F\cup\partial I\times P)$ . Similarly, $r$ determines a reflected tangle $\mathcal{T}^{R}_{ij}$ , the sequence $(\mathcal{T}_{ij},\mathcal{T}_{ij}^{R},\dots,\mathcal{T}_{ij}^{R})$ determines a solid cylindrical tangle, and doubling determines a cyclic wedge tangle. Fixing the number $2n$ , the $2n$ -replicant of the cyclic wedge tangle is the same as the $2$ -replicant of the solid cylindrical tangle, so we may define the $(2n,2)$ -replicant $D^{(2n,2)}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right)$ to be the resulting link from either replication. We say that $\mathcal{T}_{ij}$ is $(2n,2)$ -hyperbolic if $D^{(2n,2)}\left(\mathcal{T}_{ij}\right)$ is hyperbolic, in which case we define

$$ \operatorname{vol}^{(2n,2)}\left(\mathcal{T}_{ij}\right):=\frac{\operatorname{vol}\left(D^{(2n,2)}\left(\mathcal{T}_{ij}\right)\right)}{4n}. $$

See Figure 14 for a wedge tangle $\mathcal{T}$ which, when doubled one way, yields a solid-cylinder tangle, and when doubled another way, yields a cyclic wedge tangle. Each of those, when doubled, both generate $D^{(2,2)}(\mathcal{T})$ . The fact that doubling over the two sets of endpoints commute with each other is a special case of Proposition 2.13.

*Figure 14. A wedge tangle generates either a solid-cylinder tangle or a cyclic wedge tangle, each of which generates the same link in the solid torus.*

Using this notation, we have a similar result to Theorems 4.2 and 4.3, which we condense into a single theorem which follows immediately from Theorem 3.8.

#### Theorem 4.6.

Let $L\subset V$ be a link in a solid torus.

- (i) Suppose there exists a surface separating $L$ into solid-cylinder tangles $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ such that each $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ is $2$ -hyperbolic. Then $L$ is hyperbolic, and its volume satisfies

$$ \operatorname{vol}(M)\geq\sum_{i}\operatorname{vol}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right). $$

- (ii) Suppose there exists a starburst separating $L$ into $2n$ cyclic wedge tangles $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ such that each $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ is $2n$ -hyperbolic. Then $L$ is hyperbolic, and its volume satisfies

$$ \operatorname{vol}(M)\geq\sum_{i}\operatorname{vol}^{2n}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right). $$

- (iii) Suppose there is a starburst separating a solid-cylinder tangle $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ into a cycle of $2n$ wedge tangles $\mathcal{T}_{ij}$ such that each wedge tangle is $(2n,2)$ -hyperbolic. Then, $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ is $2$ -hyperbolic in the solid torus, with volume satisfying

$$ \operatorname{vol}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right)\geq\sum_{j}\operatorname{vol}^{(2n,2)}\left(\mathcal{T}_{ij}\right). $$

- (iv) Suppose there is a starburst separating a cyclic wedge tangle $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ into a cycle of wedge tangles $\mathcal{T}_{ij}$ such that each wedge tangle is $(2n,2)$ -hyperbolic in a solid torus. Then, $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ is $2n$ -hyperbolic in the solid torus, with volume satisfying

$$ \operatorname{vol}^{2n}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right)\geq\sum_{j}\operatorname{vol}^{(2n,2)}\left(\mathcal{T}_{ij}\right). $$

∎

We describe an analog to Proposition 4.4; the class of 2-hyperbolic solid-cylinder tangles is closed under composition by Theorem 3.7. Further, Corollary 3.13 implies that the composition of $n$ cyclic-wedge tangles which are each $2mn$ -hyperbolic is $2m$ -hyperbolic in the solid torus. Similar statements hold for wedge tangles, depending on which direction the composition follows.

There is a strong relationship between solid-cylinder tangles and thickened-cylinder tangles. If a solid-cylinder tangle $\mathcal{T}$ has an unknotted strand with endpoints on both components of $D\times\partial I$ , then the complement of that strand determines a thickened-cylinder tangle. The solid-cylinder tangle may be reconstructed from this thickened-cylinder tangle. The complement of the double of the solid-cylinder tangle is homeomorphic to the complement of the associated thickened-cylinder tangle, so [22] will yield a large class of examples of $2$ -hyperbolic solid-cylinder tangles.

### 4.3. Bracelet links within the sphere

#### Definition 4.7.

A saucer tangle is a tangle in the piece defined in Figure 4 which has at least two endpoints on each face and composition of saucer tangles is defined by attaching their endpoints, as in the thickened-cylinder case. As defined in the introduction, if $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ is a saucer tangle, then the length- $2n$ sequence $(\mathcal{T}_{i},\mathcal{T}_{i}^{R},\dots,\mathcal{T}_{i}^{R})$ determines a bracelet link $D^{2n}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right)\subset S^{3}$ in the 3-sphere, called it $2n$ -replicant. We say that $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ is $2n$ -hyperbolic if $D^{2n}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right)$ is a hyperbolic link, in which case we define the volume

$$ \operatorname{vol}^{2n}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right):=\frac{\operatorname{vol}\left(D^{2n}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right)\right)}{2n}. $$

#### Remark 4.8.

We make the restriction that saucer tangles have two endpoints on each face in service of Theorem 5.1. This does not fundamentally change the class of $2m$ -hyperbolic saucer tangles relative to the class of tangles without such a restriction; in the case $m\geq 2$ , any tangle with $\leq 1$ endpoints on one face will have $2m$ -replicant which is not a prime link, and hence is not hyperbolic, and in the case of a $2m=2$ hyperbolic tangle, we can choose a piece structure which has the same $2$ -replicant and has at least 2 endpoints on each face.

Unlike Theorems 4.2, 4.3, and 4.6, the intersection of the surfaces making up the evident starburst is closed in this case; hence we may directly conclude the following theorem from Theorem 2.4.

#### Theorem 4.9.

If $L$ is a bracelet link made of a cycle $(\mathcal{T}_{i})_{i=1}^{2n}$ of $2n$ saucer tangles such that each $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ is $2n$ -hyperbolic, then $L$ is hyperbolic and the volumes satisfy

$$ \operatorname{vol}(L)\geq\sum_{i}\operatorname{vol}^{2n}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right). $$

∎

Hyperbolicity of saucer tangles will be discussed further in Section 5, including composition of tangles and the relationship between $2m$ -hyperbolicity and $2m^{\prime}$ -hyperbolicity for $m,m^{\prime}$ distinct.

### 4.4. Links in $S^{2}\times S^{1}$

When we glue two solid tori together along their boundary, meridian to meridian, we obtain $S^{2}\times S^{1}$ . Given a torus lattice link $L$ projected onto the separating torus, we can glue a triangular prism from each solid torus together along a square face from each on the separating torus to obtain a thickened bigon. See Figure 15. Thus we can decompose $L$ into thickened bigon tangles.By Theorem 2.4, a similar theorem to our previous cases holds.

*Figure 15. A square tangle in a thickened bigon.*

#### Theorem 4.10.

Let $L$ be an $(2m,2n)$ -torus lattice link in $S^{2}\times S^{1}$ , consisting of $4mn$ thickened bigon tangles $\{\mathcal{T}_{ij}\}$ . If each tangle $\mathcal{T}_{ij}$ is $(2,2n)$ -hyperbolic, then $L$ is hyperbolic, and its volume satisfies

$$ \operatorname{vol}(M)\geq\sum_{i,j}\operatorname{vol}^{(2,2n)}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right). $$

## 5. Various hyperbolicities for tangles

Define a saucer tangle to be a braid if all strings of the tangle move monotonically left to right from the left face to the right face, intersecting each disk in the saucer parallel to the faces exactly once. We note that if a tangle is $2n$ -hyperbolic, then its composition with a braid is still $2n$ -hyperbolic with the same $2n$ -volume. This is immediate because the composition of an $\ell$ -string braid with its reflection yields a trivial braid of $\ell$ strings. Hence, the $2n$ -replicant of a tangle $T$ composed with a braid yields the $2n$ -replicant of $T$ alone.

#### Theorem 5.1.

Suppose $\mathcal{T}$ is a $2n$ -hyperbolic tangle in a saucer for some $n\geq 1$ . Then, $\mathcal{T}$ is $2m$ -hyperbolic for all $m\geq n$ .

#### Proof.

It suffices to prove that $\mathcal{T}$ is $2(n+1)$ -hyperbolic, which is by definition showing $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ is hyperbolic. Let $L^{\prime}$ be the link that is given by the $2(n+1)$ -replicant of $\mathcal{T}$ . So we want to show $S^{3}\setminus L^{\prime}$ is hyperbolic.

We are assuming $D^{2n}(\mathcal{T})$ is hyperbolic, which means that the link $L$ in $S^{3}$ that is the $2n$ -replicant of $\mathcal{T}$ is hyperbolic. Define $\mathbf{S}$ to be the collection of surfaces that decompose $D^{2n}(\mathcal{T})$ into homeomorphic copies of $\mathcal{T}$ , and let $E$ be the intersection set of the surfaces. Note that in the case $n=1$ , $E=\varnothing$ . Because $D^{2n}(\mathcal{T})$ is hyperbolic and reflection in any of the surfaces is a symmetry of the manifold, Theorem 1.4 implies that each surface is totally geodesic, which immediately implies it is incompressible in $D^{2n}(\mathcal{T})$ .

Let $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ be the collection of surfaces that decompose $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ into homeomorphic copies of the saucer tangle $\mathcal{T}$ . Let $E^{\prime}$ be their intersection set. Note that $E^{\prime}\neq\varnothing$ for all $n$ .

We begin the proof by showing that each surface in $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ is incompressible. Then, we will use this to prove that $L^{\prime}$ is nontrivial, and use this to prove that essential disks induce essential spheres. Then, we again use incompressibility to prove that essential spheres induce essential spheres in $D^{2n}(\mathcal{T})$ , so $2n$ -hyperbolicity precludes essential disks and spheres in $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ . Then, we prove that $L^{\prime}$ is a prime link, precluding certain essential annuli. Given a torus in $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ , we use this together with a strategy of restricting to pieces and replicating in order to prove that there are no essential tori in $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ . Lastly, we use the properties of $L^{\prime}$ already proved to show that $L^{\prime}$ is not Seifert fibered, and use [16, 5] to conclude that $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ has no essential annuli, implying that it is hyperbolic.

Each surface in $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ is incompressible. Suppose for contradiction that $\Sigma\in\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ is compressible. Choose a compressing disk $D$ for $\Sigma$ that has the least number of intersections with $E^{\prime}$ , and then the least number of simple closed curve intersections with $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ among such disks. The intersection graph of $D$ with $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ on $D$ will be a collection of arcs with both endpoints on the boundary and a collection of simple closed curves. If there is a simple closed intersection curve with a surface $\Sigma^{\prime}$ , we replace the disk $D$ with an innermost such disk on $D$ , which does not intersect any other surfaces if it exists. This contradicts the minimality of the intersection set for $D$ , so there are no simple closed curves of intersection.

If there are arcs of intersection on $D$ , choose an outermost arc of intersection on $D$ cutting a bigonal disk $D^{\prime}$ from $D$ . Then $D^{\prime}$ is a bigonal disk in a particular saucer $S_{i}$ with its edges in the faces of $S_{i}$ . If both edges are in the same face of $S_{i}$ , then when replicated in $D^{2n}(\mathcal{T})$ , it yields a set of spheres, each of which must bound balls in $S^{3}\setminus L$ . Thus we could have isotoped $D$ to eliminate intersections in $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ , a contradiction to minimality.

If the two edges of $D^{\prime}$ are on distinct faces of $S_{i}$ , replicating $D^{\prime}$ yields a sphere in $D^{2n}(\mathcal{T})$ , which must be inessential. Hence it bounds a ball. Thus $D^{\prime}$ must cut a ball from the saucer tangle in $S_{i}$ . This means that $D$ could have been isotoped to eliminate the intersection curve in $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ , contradicting minimality. This proves that the surfaces in $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ are all incompressible.

The link $L^{\prime}$ is nontrivial. Suppose first that the link $L^{\prime}$ is trivial. Then $L^{\prime}$ consists of a single component bounding a disk $D$ . By incompressibility of the surfaces in $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ , we can remove all simple closed curves of intersection with any of the surfaces with $D$ . For any surface $\Sigma$ in $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ , consider an outermost intersection arc in $D\cap\Sigma$ on $D$ . It cuts a disk $D^{\prime}$ from $D$ , the boundary of a regular neighborhood of which is a compressing disk for $\Sigma$ , since $\Sigma$ has at least four punctures by $L^{\prime}$ . Thus, $D$ and therefore the link $L^{\prime}$ cannot intersect any of the surfaces in $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ , again a contradiction to our construction. Therefore $L^{\prime}$ cannot be a trivial knot.

The manifold $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ has no essential disks or spheres. Note that for a nontrivial link, the boundary of a regular neighborhood of an essential disk in its complement is an essential sphere. Hence we can prove that there are no essential disks in $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ by proving that there are no essential spheres.

Suppose now that there is an essential sphere $S$ in $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ . Because of the incompressibility of the surfaces in $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ , we can isotope the sphere to miss each in turn until it misses all of the surfaces. Hence, it now resides in a single saucer. Thus, there is a copy $S^{\prime}$ that exists in $D^{2n}(\mathcal{T})$ (in fact $2n$ copies). But in $D^{2n}(\mathcal{T})$ , $S^{\prime}$ must bound a ball. Hence it bounds a ball in the single saucer. Thus, $S$ bounds a ball in $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ , a contradiction to the essentiality of the sphere.

The link $L^{\prime}$ is prime. Before moving on to essential tori, we first prove that the link $L^{\prime}$ in $S^{3}$ is prime. Suppose not, and let $S$ be the essential (incompressible, boundary-incompressible) twice punctured sphere in the complement of $L^{\prime}$ . Consider its intersections with the surfaces in $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ , and assume we have chosen $S$ to have a minimum number of intersection curves. If it intersects one of the surfaces $\Sigma$ in a closed curve that is trivial on the punctured sphere, then we can isotope to remove the intersection. If it intersects one of the surfaces in a closed curve that is nontrivial on the punctured sphere and that avoids the axis of the starburst on $\Sigma$ , and all intersection curves avoid the axis, then taking an innermost such on $S$ yields a disk $D$ that is once-punctured on $S$ and that is properly embedded in a single saucer. This reflects to a twice-punctured sphere $S^{\prime}$ in $D^{2n}(\mathcal{T})$ , which must then bound an unknotted arc to one side in $L$ since $L$ must be prime. If $n\geq 2$ , then there are multiple such twice-punctured spheres so it must be that they contain a trivial arc to the inside. However, then $D$ cuts a ball from the saucer in which it lies which contains an unknotted arc in $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ , and we can isotope $D$ to remove the intersection, contradicting minimality of the number of intersection curves.

If $n=1$ , it could be that the unknotted arc is to the outside of $S^{\prime}$ . But then the opposite face of the saucer contains only one endpoint of the tangle, a contradiction to our assumption that the number of endpoints of the tangles in a face is at least two.

Finally, suppose that $S$ intersects a surface $\Sigma$ in a curve nontrivial on $S$ that intersects the axis $E^{\prime}$ of the starburst on $\Sigma$ . Then $S$ intersects all of the surfaces in $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ . The set of intersection arcs forms a $2(n+1)$ -valent graph on $S$ with an even number of vertices. Choose a component of this graph that is innermost on $S$ , in the sense that all of its complementary regions but one do not contain further components of the graph. Dropping the other components of the graph, we now have a connected $2(n+1)$ -valent graph on $S$ with an even number of vertices.

In fact, there can be no odd cycles in $G$ . This is because the cyclic order of pieces around a vertex must be preserved. Hence, for any edge in $G$ , the cyclic orders must be clockwise around one endpoint and counterclockwise around the other. In particular, this means $G$ must be a bipartite graph, with all even-length cycles.

For such a graph on a sphere, define $f_{2n}$ to be the number of complementary faces with $2n$ edges. Then if $v$ , $e$ and $f$ are the number of vertices, edges and faces, by Euler characteristic, we know $v-e+f=2$ , where $e=(n+1)v$ , so $-\frac{n}{n+1}e+f=2$ . However,

$$ f=f_{2}+f_{4}+f_{6}+\dots $$

and

$$ e=\frac{2f_{2}+4f_{4}+6f_{6}+\dots}{2} $$

Plugging these into the Euler equation and algebra yields:

$$ \frac{f_{2}}{n+1}+\frac{1-n}{n+1}f_{4}+\frac{1-2n}{n+1}f_{6}+\dots=2 $$

Thus,

$$ f_{2}\geq 2(n+1)\geq 4 $$

At most two of the at least four bigonal faces can be punctured, since $S$ has only two punctures, so there is a bigonal disk face $D^{\prime}$ that is not punctured. Then by the same argument as before (replicating in $D^{2n}(\mathcal{T})$ to obtain a sphere which must bound a ball), we can isotope $S$ in $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ to lower the number of intersections, a contradiction to our choice of $S$ . Thus $L^{\prime}$ is prime in $S^{3}$ .

The manifold $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ has no essential tori. Suppose now that there is an essential torus $T$ in $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ . By the incompressibility of the surfaces in $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ , we can isotope $T$ to eliminate any trivial intersection curves on the torus with any of the surfaces in $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ .

We first consider the case that the torus does not intersect the axis of the starburst. Then $T$ intersects the collection of surfaces $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ in a finite collection of parallel curves on $T$ . Assume we have chosen $T$ to have a minimal number of these intersections. These curves divide $T$ into a finite collection of annuli $\{A_{i}\}$ which are properly embedded in $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})\backslash\backslash\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ . If there is an annulus $A_{i}$ in a given saucer $S_{i}$ with its boundaries on the same copy of a surface $\Sigma$ from $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ , then it replicates in $D^{2n}(\mathcal{T})$ to a collection of tori, each made up of two copies of the annulus, and each of which cannot be essential. Let $T^{\prime}$ be one of these tori. Then it is either boundary-parallel or it is compressible. If it is boundary-parallel, the annulus $A_{i}$ is boundary-parallel to a segment of a link component in the saucer $S_{i}$ . Then meridianally compressing $T$ in $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ either yields an essential annulus, contradicting primeness of $L^{\prime}$ or it shows that $T$ was in fact boundary-parallel, also a contradiction.

If $T^{\prime}$ is compressible, then there is a disk $D$ that realizes the compression with boundary a longitude on $T^{\prime}$ . The disk $D$ can be isotoped to intersect a single saucer in a disk with boundary one arc a nontrivial arc on the annulus $A_{i}$ and the other arc on the boundary of the saucer. Hence, we can isotope a nontrivial arc on the annulus $A_{i}$ into the neighboring saucer, leaving a disk from $T$ still in $S_{i}$ . By incompressibility, we can eliminate this intersection, a contradiction to minimality of the intersection curves.

Thus, all annuli $A_{i}$ have their two boundaries on two different faces of each saucer. Since a pair of adjacent saucers and tangles are homeomorphic via reflection, we can consider $A_{i}$ and $A_{i+1}^{R}$ in the same saucer $S_{i}$ . Note that both $A_{i}$ and $A_{i+1}^{R}$ share one boundary component on the face $F_{1}$ of $\partial S_{i}$ .

We now isotope $A_{i}$ and $A_{i+1}^{R}$ into general position and consider intersection curves between them. These can take the form of arcs or simple closed curves. If there is a simple closed curve intersection, then if it is trivial on both annuli, by taking innermost such curves, the disks cut from them form a sphere in $S_{i}$ . But as $S_{i}$ appears in $D^{2n}(\mathcal{T})$ , this sphere must bound a ball. Hence we can isotope to remove the intersection curve. If one of the two curves is trivial, this contradicts the incompressibility of the torus. We consider the case that both are nontrivial shortly.

*Figure 16. The two annuli $A_{i}$ and $A_{i+1}^{R}$ can intersect in various ways.*

Suppose there is an intersection arc beginning and ending on their shared boundary, as in Figure 16(a). Then it must cut a disk from each and again, we can form a sphere that allows us to isotope the intersection away.

Suppose there is an intersection curve that runs from the shared boundary on $F_{1}$ to the opposite boundary on each of $A_{i}$ and $A_{i+1}^{R}$ on $F_{2}$ , as in Figure 16(b). Then the opposite boundaries must cross each other on $F_{2}$ , so there must be an even number of such curves. Then a pair of disks on the annuli cut from two adjacent vertical arcs on each share their bottom edge and their two vertical edges. Together they form a disk with boundary in $F_{2}$ . When we take the neighboring saucer, this disk doubles to a sphere, which appears in these two copies of the saucer and hence in $D^{2n}(\mathcal{T})$ . But it must bound a ball in $D^{2n}(\mathcal{T})$ and hence in $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ . Thus, we can isotope the annuli to eliminate these two intersection curves.

So there are now no intersection arcs that end on the shared boundary of the two annuli. Suppose that there is a simple closed curve of intersection. As shown above, it must be nontrivial on both annuli, as in Figure 16(c). Taking the two annuli it cuts from $A_{i}$ and $A_{i+1}^{R}$ that share their shared boundary, we can construct a torus living in $S_{i}$ , with a longitude on the boundary of $S_{i}$ . Since $S_{i}$ appears in $D^{2n}(\mathcal{T})$ , this torus $T^{\prime}$ must either compress or be boundary parallel there. Because $A_{i}$ and $A_{i+1}^{R}$ are incompressible, $T^{\prime}$ cannot compress to the outside. If it compresses to the inside, then it compresses to a sphere $S^{\prime}\subset S_{i}$ , which must bound a ball; hence $T^{\prime}$ bounds a solid torus in $S_{i}$ , and we can isotope $A_{i+1}^{R}$ to $A_{i}$ , eliminating the intersection curve.

If $T^{\prime}$ is boundary parallel, then there is a link component that forms the core curve for the solid torus bounded by $T^{\prime}$ . But this link component wraps once around both annuli. When we reflect $S_{i}$ in $D^{2n}(\mathcal{T})$ , this link component is reflected to a second copy that is parallel to the first. That is, they will form the boundary of an annulus that follows either $A_{i}$ and its reflection or $A_{i+1}$ and its reflection, contradicting the hyperbolicity of $D^{2n}(\mathcal{T})$ . Thus there are no simple closed curves of intersection.

The final possibility for intersection curves are arcs of intersection that end on the other unshared boundaries of the two annuli, as in Figure 16(d). These must cut disks from the two annuli. Together these two disks form a disk with boundary on $F_{2}$ . By incompressibilty, we know that this disk together with the disk it cuts from $F_{2}$ bounds a ball, and therefore we can isotope the two annuli to eliminate the intersection.

Thus, we now have no intersections curves. The union of the two annuli forms a new annulus, the reflected double over $F_{2}$ of which is a torus $T^{\prime\prime}$ . That torus exists in $D^{2n}(\mathcal{T})$ and therefore it must either be boundary parallel or compressible there. If it is boundary parallel there, there is a single link component inside it that forms the core curve for the solid torus bounded by $T^{\prime\prime}$ . But this contradicts the fact $T^{\prime\prime}$ was obtained by reflection doubling. If $T^{\prime\prime}$ is compressible then it must bound a solid torus with no components inside it. Therefore $A_{i+1}^{R}$ is isotopic to $A_{i}$ .

Thus we see that the original torus $T$ can be isotoped so that all of the $A_{i}$ are the same in each $S_{i}$ . That is, the torus is made up of $A_{1},A_{1}^{R},A_{1},\dots,A_{1}^{R}$ , in the respective copies of $S_{1}$ and $S_{1}^{R}$ , making up $D^{2(n+1)}({\mathcal{T}})$ .

Consider the corresponding torus $T^{\prime\prime\prime}$ in $D^{2n}(\mathcal{T})$ . It consists of $2n$ copies of $A_{1}$ . It must be either boundary-parallel or compressible. if it is boundary-parallel the solid cylinder bounded by $A_{1}$ contains a core curve that is an arc in a link component. But then $T$ is also boundary-parallel in $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ .

If $T^{\prime\prime\prime}$ is compressible in $D^{2n}(\mathcal{T})$ , the compression must be to the outside. Thus, there is a compressing disk $D$ which we can choose to minimize the intersection curves with $\mathbf{S}$ and such that its boundary is a longitude on $T^{\prime\prime\prime}$ . By incompressibility of the surfaces, we can isotope it so that it has a single arc of intersection with each surface $\Sigma_{i}$ and all of those arcs meet at the intersection of the surfaces.
