Then take $D^{\prime}$ to be its intersection with saucer $S_{1}$ . If we then take the union of the copies of $D^{\prime}$ and its reflections, we obtain a compressing disk for $T$ in $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ . Thus there are no essential tori that avoid $E$ in $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ .

Suppose now that there is an essential torus in $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ that intersects the axis $E$ of the starburst. We take the essential torus with the least number of intersections with $E$ , and then with the least number of curves of intersection with $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ . Since $E$ is the only place that any two of the surfaces intersect and all the surfaces intersect there, the collection of intersection curves of $T$ with $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ forms a graph $G$ on $T$ with an even number of vertices, each of valency $2(n+1)\geq 4$ . Since $T$ intersects each surface in a disjoint set of curves, each surface $\Sigma_{i}$ intersects $T$ in a parallel set of $(p_{i},q_{i})$ -curves.

If there is a component of $G$ that lies in either a disk or annulus on $T$ , then as in the case of an essential sphere that intersects $E^{\prime}$ , there is a complementary region to $G$ that is a bigon, and this generates a sphere in $D^{2n}(\mathcal{T})$ that bounds a ball, and that then allows us to isotope $T$ to reduce the number of intersections with $E^{\prime}$ in $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ , a contradiction.

So $G$ must consist of a single component such that all of its complementary regions are disks.

We use a similar argument in the proof of Lemma 3.5. As mentioned previously, $G$ cannot have any bigonal complementary regions. This forces $n=1$ or $n=2$ . In the second case, there are three surfaces in $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ and and all complementary regions on $T$ are triangles. However, as mentioned previously, there can be no odd cycles in $G$ , as cyclic order must be preserved between different vertices.

So $n=1$ and there are two surfaces in $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ , each a punctured sphere. $T$ intersects each one in a collection of curves. Taking an innermost such curve on the sphere, we know it bounds a disk in $S^{3}$ intersecting $T$ only in its boundary. So it must either be a meridian or a longitude. Since the two sets of curves cannot be parallel, as otherwise they would generate a bigon, one set consists of meridians and the other of longitudes, and $T$ is an unknotted torus in $S^{3}$ . If we take any square $Q$ complementary to $G$ on $T$ , it is properly embedded in $\mathcal{T}$ and $\partial Q$ crosses $E$ four times. It doubles to a sphere living in $D^{2n}(\mathcal{T})=D(\mathcal{T})$ , which by hyperbolicity, bounds a ball. So to one side of $Q$ in $\mathcal{T}$ , there are no link arcs. Therefore, we can isotope a properly embedded arc in $Q$ to $E$ . We can use this fact to isotope $T$ in $D^{4}(\mathcal{T})$ to lower the number of intersections with $E$ , a contradiction to our choice of $T$ .

The manifold $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ has no essential annuli. We now consider an essential annulus $A$ in $D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ . Lemma 1.16 of [16], shows that if a manifold is connected, orientable, irreducible and atoroidal, which we have shown our link complement to be, then the existence of an incompressible boundary-incompressible annulus implies the manifold is Seifert fibered. In [5], a complete determination of link complements in $S^{3}$ that are Seifert fibered is given. In particular, the only options that are nontrivial, prime, and that have no essential tori are a Hopf link, or a $(p,q)$ -torus knot $K$ , with annulus on the defining torus, and possibly with one or both of the core curves of the solid tori to either side of the torus, denoted $\alpha_{1}$ and $\alpha_{2}$ , included as well.

There are no spheres in $S^{3}$ that become incompressible punctured spheres in the Hopf link complement. So $L^{\prime}$ is a torus knot with possibly two additional components as described.

If neither core curve is present, so we are in a torus knot complement, then there are no incompressible punctured spheres to play the role of the surfaces in $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ ([24]). In the case that $\alpha_{1}$ or $\alpha_{2}$ are present, the $(p,q)$ -torus knot $K$ lies on a torus $T$ defined by the annulus $A$ , with a solid torus or a cored solid torus to each side.

Since the fundamental groups of a solid torus and cored solid torus are $\mathbf{Z}$ or $\mathbf{Z}\times\mathbf{Z}$ , and a planar surface has fundamental group a free product of $\mathbf{Z}$ ’s, the only incompressible sub-surfaces of our punctured sphere properly embedded in either one are a disk, a once-punctured disk whose puncture corresponds with a puncture of $\Sigma$ , and an annulus whose boundaries are not punctures of $\Sigma$ . But note that the boundaries of any of these surfaces can intersect the punctures on $\Sigma$ since they may cross the $(p,q)$ -torus knot on $T$ . Thus, an incompressible punctured sphere $\Sigma\subset D^{2(n+1)}(\mathcal{T})$ can only intersect each side in a disjoint union of disks, once-punctured disks, or annuli. In the case of the annulus, both boundaries are on $T$ , and the annulus is boundary-parallel to $T$ .

If there is a disk $D$ that has boundary trivial on $T$ , then it cuts a ball $B$ from that side of $T$ . If there are no further components of $\Sigma\setminus(\Sigma\cap T)$ inside the ball, then either $\partial D$ intersects $L^{\prime}$ or it does not. If not, we can isotope $\Sigma$ to decrease the number of intersections with $T$ . If it does, then we can isotope an arc of $L^{\prime}$ to $D$ while fixing it endpoints, implying $\Sigma$ is boundary-compressible and hence compressible.

If there is another component of $\Sigma\setminus(\Sigma\cap T)$ in $B$ , we can take an innermost such. It cannot be a punctured disk. If it is a disk, the argument just given eliminates it. If it is an annulus $A^{\prime}$ , that annulus must have boundaries trivial on $T$ , and that annulus cuts a solid torus $V$ off of that side of $T$ . If $\partial A^{\prime}$ does not intersect $L^{\prime}$ , we can isotope $A^{\prime}$ to eliminate the intersections with $T$ . If it does intersect $L^{\prime}$ then there is an arc of $L^{\prime}$ that can be isotoped fixing its endpoints into $A^{\prime}$ , once again contradicting incompressibility of $\Sigma$ .

A similar argument eliminates all annuli in $\Sigma\setminus(\Sigma\cap T)$ with boundary trivial in $T$ by taking an innermost such and applying the argument already given.

By taking an innermost curve of intersection of $\Sigma\cap T$ on $\Sigma$ , there is a disk or punctured disk to one side of $T$ , and it must have meridianal boundary in the solid torus or cored solid torus to that side of $T$ .

Hence, to the other side, there must be an annulus $A^{\prime}$ with boundaries that are longitudinal in the solid torus or cored solid torus to that side. Such an annulus splits the solid torus or cored solid tori into two solid tori, at most one of which can contain the possibly missing core. To that side, take an innermost such annulus $A^{\prime\prime}$ . That annulus is boundary-parallel to $T$ , and if its boundary misses $L^{\prime}$ , we can eliminate the intersections. If its boundaries intersect $L^{\prime}$ , then we can isotope an arc of $L^{\prime}$ into $A^{\prime}$ , contradicting incompressibility of $\Sigma$ .

∎

#### Remark 5.2.

Though Theorem 5.1 may extend to other special classes of pieces, it is not true for all pieces. For instance, the restriction that saucer tangles have at least two endpoints on each face is necessary. If we allowed a saucer tangle that had only one endpoint on a face, we could still choose the tangle so that it is 2-hyperbolic. But it will never be $2m$ -hyperbolic for any $m>1$ as it will not yield a prime knot or link.

Another example where Theorem 5.1 fails to extend comes from Lemma 3.5. Given a $4$ -hyperbolic piece $P$ whose $4$ -replicant has an intersection locus intersecting a torus boundary component, its $2m$ -replicant also has an intersection locus intersecting a torus boundary component. Hence Lemma 3.5 implies that $P$ is not $2m$ -hyperbolic for any $m>2$ .

We gain the following useful corollary.

#### Corollary 5.3.

Suppose $\{\mathcal{T}_{j}\}$ is a collection of $n$ $2m$ -hyperbolic saucer tangles such that the composition $\mathcal{T}_{i}\circ\mathcal{T}_{i+1}$ is defined for all $i$ . Then, $\mathcal{T}_{1}\circ\mathcal{T}_{2}\circ\cdots\circ\mathcal{T}_{n}$ is $2m$ -hyperbolic.

#### Proof.

Theorem 5.1 implies that each $\mathcal{T}_{j}$ is $2mn$ -hyperbolic, hence Corollary 3.13 implies that the composition is $2m$ -hyperbolic. ∎

The analogy to tangles in $T\times I$ carries to the following theorems.

#### Theorem 5.4.

Suppose $L$ is a bracelet link made of a cycle $(\mathcal{T}_{i})_{i=1}^{n}$ of $n\geq 2m$ saucer tangles such that each $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ is $2m$ -hyperbolic. Then, $L$ is hyperbolic. If $n=2m$ , then the volume satisfies

$$ \operatorname{vol}(L)\geq\sum_{i}\operatorname{vol}^{2n}\left(\mathcal{T}_{i}\right). $$

∎

#### Theorem 5.5.

Suppose $\mathcal{T}$ is a tetrahedral tangle that is $(2m,2n)$ -hyperbolic for some $m,n\geq 1$ . Then, $\mathcal{T}$ is $(2r,2s)$ -hyperbolic for all $r\geq m$ and $s\geq n$ .

#### Proof.

The $(2m,2n)$ -replicant of $\mathcal{T}$ can be decomposed into $2m$ saucer tangles, each consisting of $n$ copies of $\mathcal{T}$ and $n$ copies of its reflection. But then the fact the $(2m,2n)$ -replicant of $\mathcal{T}$ is hyperbolic is equivalent to the fact the $2n$ -replicant of the saucer tangle is hyperbolic. But then we know the $2s$ -replicant of the saucer tangle is hyperbolic by the theorem, so $\mathcal{T}$ is $(2m,2s)$ -hyperbolic. We can repeat the process, only this time decomposing into $2s$ saucer tangles, each consisting of $m$ copies of $\mathcal{T}$ and $m$ copies of its reflection. Again the theorem implies that this saucer tangle is $2r$ -hyperbolic, implying that $\mathcal{T}$ is $(2r,2s)$ -hyperbolic.

∎

In the case of bracelet links, $2$ -hyperbolicity of some classes of saucer tangles have been previously studied. We consider one such class here.

### 6.1. Arborescent tangles

Rational tangles, as defined by Conway in [8] are examples of saucer tangles. We can think of a rational tangle as constructed by starting with either the 0 tangle corresponding to two horizontal strands or the $\infty$ tangle corresponding to two vertical strands.Then we alternately twist the right two endpoints and the the bottom two endpoints to create a link in the 3-ball. Note that when we start, there is a disk $D$ known as the defining disk of the rational tangle, that is properly embedded in the ball and that separates the two strands. It continues to exist as we twist the endpoints, but its boundary becomes more complicated on the boundary of the ball.

Given a rational tangle in a ball, we can choose a disk $D^{\prime}$ on the boundary of the ball that contains two of the endpoints of the tangle, called a composition disk. Then given two such rational tangles with choices of disks on the boundary, we can compose the tangles by gluing the one disk to the other.

A Montesinos tangle is obtained by composing rational tangles in a row, left to right, our composition disks either being the leftside disk or the rightside disk. Arborescent tangle are defined to include rational tangles and the compositions of arborescent tangles along any composition disks.

We use previous results to determine the $2n$ -hyperbolicity of all arborescent tangles.

Let $Q_{m}$ be the arborescent tangles defined in Figure 17. We say that an arborescent tangle $\mathcal{T}$ contains $Q_{m}$ if there is a 4-times punctured sphere in $D\times I\setminus\mathcal{T}$ , called a Conway sphere, cutting $\mathcal{T}$ into two tangles, one of which is $Q_{m}$ . We say that a link contains $Q_{m}$ if it possesses such a Conway sphere.

The following Theorem was proved in [21, Thm. 3.22]. It is related to a theorem originally in an unpublished manuscript by Bonahon and Siebenmann (see [4]), also proved in [21] and [11] by essentially different means.

#### Theorem 6.1 ([21]).

Suppose $\mathcal{T}$ is an arborescent tangle. Then, $\mathcal{T}$ is $2$ -hyperbolic if and only if none of the following hold:

- (1) $\mathcal{T}$ is a rational tangle.

- (2) $\mathcal{T}=Q_{m}\circ\mathcal{T}^{\prime}$ or $\mathcal{T}=\mathcal{T}^{\prime}\circ Q_{m}$ for some $m\geq 1$ and some arborescent tangle $\mathcal{T}^{\prime}$ .

- (3) $\mathcal{T}$ contains $Q_{m}$ for some $m\geq 2$ .

∎

Note that a rational tangle $\mathcal{T}$ can never be 2-hyperbolic since the defining disk doubles to a separating sphere for the resulting link.

We will use this theorem and Corollary 3.13 to determine $2n$ -hyperbolicity. In order to state the result, we define a saucer tangle $\mathcal{T}$ to be principally $2n$ -hyperbolic if it is $2n$ hyperbolic and either $n=1$ or $\mathcal{T}$ is not $2(n-1)$ -hyperbolic. We say that a saucer tangle is entirely non-hyperbolic if it is not $2n$ -hyperbolic for any $n$ .

#### Corollary 6.2.

Suppose $\mathcal{T}$ is an arborescent tangle. Then, $\mathcal{T}$ is entirely non-hyperbolic if and only if one of the following hold:

- (1) $\mathcal{T}$ is an integer tangle.

- (2) $\mathcal{T}=Q_{m}\circ\mathcal{T}^{\prime}$ or $\mathcal{T}=\mathcal{T}^{\prime}\circ Q_{m}$ for some $m\geq 1$ .

- (3) $\mathcal{T}$ contains $Q_{m}$ for some $m\geq 2$ .

Further, $\mathcal{T}$ is principally 2-hyperbolic if and only if none of these hold and $\mathcal{T}$ is non-rational. Moreover, $\mathcal{T}$ is principally 4-hyperbolic if and only if it is a non-integer rational tangle other than $Q_{\text{clasp}}.$ Last, $\mathcal{T}$ is principally 6-hyperbolic if and only if it is equal to $Q_{\text{clasp}}.$

We use the fact (see [17]), that a sum of two rational tangles is rational if and only if one of the two is an integer tangle.

#### Proof of Corollary 6.2.

We first assume that $\mathcal{T}$ is an arborescent tangle satisfying one of (1)-(3), and we show that $\mathcal{T}\circ\mathcal{T}^{R}\cdots\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}$ satisfies one of the conditions of Theorem (6.1), where $\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}$ stands for either $\mathcal{T}$ or $\mathcal{T}^{R}$ depending on the parity.

Suppose that $\mathcal{T}$ is an integer tangle. Then, by the preceding discussion, we see inductively that

$$ \mathcal{T}\circ\mathcal{T}^{R}\cdots\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}=\mathcal{T}\circ\left(\mathcal{T}^{R}\cdots\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}\right) $$

is a rational tangle (in fact an integer tangle). Hence Theorem 6.1 implies that no such tangles are 2-hyperbolic, so 3.13 implies that $\mathcal{T}$ is entirely non-hyperbolic.

Suppose instead that $\mathcal{T}=Q_{m}\circ\mathcal{T}^{\prime}$ or $\mathcal{T}^{\prime}\circ Q_{m}$ for some $m\geq 1$ . Then, $\mathcal{T}^{R}\circ\mathcal{T}\cdots\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}$ contains $Q_{2m}$ , so we may assume that condition (3) holds. In fact, if condition (3) holds for $\mathcal{T}$ , then it holds for $\mathcal{T}\circ\mathcal{T}^{R}\cdots\widetilde{\mathcal{T}}$ , so Theorem 6.1 and Corollary 3.13 together imply that $\mathcal{T}$ is entirely non-hyperbolic.

The corollary for principal 2-hyperbolicity is a restatement of Theorem 6.1. For 4-hyperbolicity, note that $\mathcal{T}$ is not an integer tangle, so $\mathcal{T}^{R}$ is also not an integer tangle. Hence $\mathcal{T}\circ\mathcal{T}^{R}$ is not a rational tangle.

Since $Q_{m}$ contains more than two components, any rational tangle satisfies conditions (2) and (3). Further, conditions (2), (3) together imply that $\mathcal{T}$ neither contains $Q_{m}$ for $m\geq 2$ nor attains equality with $Q_{m}\circ T$ or $T\circ Q_{m}$ for $m\geq 1$ . Hence $\mathcal{T}\circ\mathcal{T}^{R}$ is 2-hyperbolic and $\mathcal{T}$ is not 2-hyperbolic. Hence $\mathcal{T}$ is principally 4-hyperbolic.

The corollary is well-known for $Q_{\text{clasp}}$ (see for instance [20]). ∎

### 6.2. Alternating tangles

We now explore a class of 2-hyperbolic solid cylindrical tangles related to alternating saucer tangles.

#### Definition 6.3.

A saucer tangle $\mathcal{T}$ is an alternating tangle if it possesses a projection to a cross-sectional bigon of the saucer such that the crossings alternate along every strand.

Since they are topologically indistinguishable, a saucer tangle $\mathcal{T}$ determines a canonical solid-cylinder tangle $\mathcal{T}_{C}$ . We show the following:

#### Proposition 6.4.

Suppose $\mathcal{T}$ is a $2m$ -hyperbolic alternating saucer tangle which intersects each end at two points. Then, $\mathcal{T}_{C}$ is a 2-hyperbolic solid-cylinder tangle with volume satisfying

$$ \operatorname{vol}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T}_{C}\right)>\operatorname{vol}^{2m}\left(\mathcal{T}\right). $$

We use the following construction.

#### Definition 6.5.

A saucer tangle $\mathcal{T}$ determines another saucer tangle $\widehat{\mathcal{T}}$ with a projection identical to that of $\mathcal{T}$ except that all crossings are switched between under-crossings and over-crossings. Using this, the length $2m$ cycle $\left(\mathcal{T},\widehat{\mathcal{T}}^{R},\dots,\widehat{\mathcal{T}}^{R}\right)$ determines an alternating bracelet link $D^{2m}_{\text{mod}}(\mathcal{T})$ , called the modified $2m$ -replicant.

If $\mathcal{T}$ is $2m$ -hyperbolic, then $\widehat{\mathcal{T}}$ is as well, and by Theorem 4.9, the link $D^{2m}_{\text{mod}}\left(\mathcal{T}\right)$ is also hyperbolic, with volume satisfying

$$ \operatorname{vol}\left(D^{2m}_{\text{mod}}{\mathcal{T}}\right)>2m\operatorname{vol}^{2m}\left(\mathcal{T}\right) $$

#### Proof of Proposition 6.4.

The link $D^{2m}_{\text{mod}}(\mathcal{T})$ is alternating by construction. Since it is hyperbolic, it must be nonsplit, prime and it must not be a torus link.

Using this, we may construct a generalized augmented alternating link by adding in a single unknotted component along the central axis of the bracelet link $D^{2m}_{\text{mod}}(\mathcal{T})$ . By [2], this link is hyperbolic, and by [23, Theorem 3.4(c)] , its volume is greater than the volume of $D^{2m}_{\text{mod}}(\mathcal{T})$ . In fact, the complement of this link is homeomorphic to that of the link in the open solid torus determined by $\left(\mathcal{T}_{C},\widehat{\mathcal{T}}^{R}_{C},\dots,\widehat{\mathcal{T}}^{R}_{C}\right)$ . Call this link $D^{2m}_{\text{mod}}(\mathcal{T}_{C})$ .

There is a collection of disjoint twice-punctured meridianal disks in the open solid torus which separate the copies of $\mathcal{T}_{C}$ and $\widehat{\mathcal{T}}^{R}_{C}$ in $D^{2m}_{\text{mod}}(\mathcal{T}_{C})$ from the rest of the link. By [1], these twice-punctured disks are totally geodesic, and cutting and then regluing along any subset of them will yield another hyperbolic manifold. In particular, $\mathcal{T}_{C}$ is 2-hyperbolic. Since $\operatorname{vol}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T}_{C}\right)=\operatorname{vol}^{2}\left(\widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{C}^{R}\right)$ , Theorem 4.6 implies that $\operatorname{vol}\left(D^{2m}_{\text{mod}}(\mathcal{T}_{C})\right)=2m\operatorname{vol}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T}_{C}\right)$ . We may summarize these inequalities as follows:

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{vol}^{2m}\left(\mathcal{T}\right) \displaystyle=\frac{\operatorname{vol}\left(D^{2m}(\mathcal{T})\right)}{2m} \displaystyle\leq\frac{\operatorname{vol}\left(D^{2m}_{\text{mod}}(\mathcal{T})\right)}{2m} \displaystyle<\frac{\operatorname{vol}\left(D^{2m}_{\text{mod}}(\mathcal{T}_{C})\right)}{2m} \displaystyle=\operatorname{vol}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T}_{C}\right). $$

∎

Note that because the twice-punctured meridianal disks are totally geodesic, the link $J$ obtained by taking a single copy of $\mathcal{T}$ , and gluing its left endpoints to its right endpoints (generating a “bracelet link” of length 1) and then removing a single unknotted component corresponding to the axis of the bracelet link is hyperbolic and its volume is equal to $\operatorname{vol}^{2}\left(\mathcal{T}_{C}\right)$ . A corollary applies to Montesinos tangles.

#### Corollary 6.6.

Let $\mathcal{T}_{C}$ be a non-integer Montesinos tangle in a solid cylinder. Then $\mathcal{T}_{C}$ is 2-hyperbolic.

#### Proof.

Let $\mathcal{T}$ be the corresponding Montesinos tangle in a saucer. Then, $\mathcal{T}$ decomposes into a composition of non-integer rational tangles (by including an integer tangle on the tail end of the preceding rational tangle if necessary). By Corollary 6.2 these are $2m$ -hyperbolic for some $m$ , and by [17] they are alternating. Since $\mathcal{T}_{C}\circ\mathcal{T}^{\prime}_{C}=(\mathcal{T}\circ\mathcal{T}^{\prime})_{C}$ , this implies that $\mathcal{T}_{C}$ decomposes into $2$ -hyperbolic solid cylindrical tangles. Then, Theorem 3.8 implies that $\mathcal{T}_{C}$ is 2-hyperbolic, as desired. ∎

## 7. Application to Other Tangle Reflection Graphs

Up to now, we have used the cyclic graph on $2n$ vertices or the $(2n,2m)$ -torus lattice graph to create links. We defined the replicants of a given tangle $\mathcal{T}$ in terms of the link obtained by alternately reflecting the tangle $\mathcal{T}$ around the graph.

We now generalize the construction. Let $G$ be a finite connected $r$ -valent bipartite graph with bipartition of the vertices into two sets $U$ and $V$ such that $G$ is embedded in an orientable 3-manifold $M$ . Let $\mathbf{S}$ a collection of surfaces in $M$ , each intersecting $G$ transversely at a subset of the edges such that for each such surface $\Sigma$ , there is an orientation-reversing involution of $M$ , which we call a reflection, with fixed point set $\Sigma$ . Further, assume that for each pair of vertices sharing an edge, there is a distinguished such reflection that switches the two vertices, sends $G$ back to itself, switches $U$ and $V$ and sends the collection $\mathbf{S}$ back to itself. Further assume that in the finite group $\mathcal{G}$ generated by the collection of reflections, the only element that fixes a vertex is the trivial element. Then we call $(M,G,\mathbf{S})$ a reflection graph of $M$ . The group $\mathcal{G}$ is fully determined as the group of isometries of $M$ generated by reflections about $\mathbf{S}$ .

Let $L$ be a link formed by inserting tangles $\mathcal{T}_{1},\mathcal{T}_{2},\dots,\mathcal{T}_{2n}$ into the $2n$ vertices of $G$ such that the nonzero number of outgoing strands along each edge match up from the two vertices. For each such tangle $\mathcal{T}$ , we can form the $G$ -replicant $D^{G}(\mathcal{T})$ of the tangle by removing all tangles except for it and then using the reflections to reflect $\mathcal{T}$ across each outgoing edge. Then we repeat the process with all subsequent edges.

To see that the definition of the replicant is well-defined, we need to show that there are $r$ distinct edge classes at each vertex under the action of $\mathcal{G}$ . Suppose not, and that there is a nontrivial element $\mu$ of $\mathcal{G}$ that identified two edges that share a vertex $y$ . Then since $\mu$ cannot fix $y$ , it must send the other endpoint of the first edge, call it $x$ to $y$ and $y$ to the other endpoint of the second edge, call it $z$ .

But because $y$ and $z$ share an edge, there must be a reflection $\lambda$ that sends $y$ to $z$ and $z$ to $y$ . But then $\lambda\circ\mu(y)=y$ . hence, $\lambda\circ\mu$ must be the identity so $\mu=\lambda^{-1}=\lambda$ . But $\lambda$ sends $z$ to $y$ whereas $\mu$ sends $x$ to $y$ , a contradiction.

The fact there are exactly $r$ equivalence classes of edges follows by reflecting to get from one vertex to an adjacent one. Then the $r$ equivalence classes with representatives at the first vertex will generate representatives of the same classes at the next vertex. Repeating for adjacent vertices will eventually make this true at all vertices.

Since the graph is bipartite, each cycle is even and this construction is well-defined. If the complement of the $G$ -replicant of $\mathcal{T}$ is hyperbolic, we say $\mathcal{T}$ is a $G$ -hyperbolic tangle with volume $\operatorname{vol}(D^{G}(\mathcal{T}))/|G|$ .

If we have a combinatorial proof that a collection of $2n$ copies of the $G$ -replicants for the tangles can be cut and reglued, always along totally geodesic surfaces, in order to obtain $2n$ copies of $M\setminus L$ , then we know that the analog of Theorem 4.9 applies. That is to say that under these circumstances, if each tangle we insert at the vertices of the graph is $G$ -hyperbolic, then the resulting link is hyperbolic with volume greater than the sum of $1/2n$ times the volumes of the $G$ -replicas. Under these circumstances, we say that $(M,G,\mathbf{S})$ is a tangle reflection graph for $M$ .

#### Theorem 7.1.

Let $(M,G,\mathbf{S})$ be a tangle reflection graph with $2n$ vertices in a compact orientable 3-manifold $M$ with possible torus boundaries. If there is a orientation-reversing symmetry $\phi$ of $M$ with fixed point set an orientable surface $S$ , such that $G$ lies in $S$ and $\phi$ preserves each surface in $\mathbf{S}$ , then there exists a new tangle reflection graph $(M,G^{\prime},\mathbf{S}^{\prime})$ for $M$ , where $G^{\prime}$ is the product of $G$ with the graph $P_{1}$ consisting of one edge and two vertices and $\mathbf{S}^{\prime}$ is the collection $\mathbf{S}$ together with the surface $S$ .

#### Proof.

Push $G$ off $S$ in a choice of normal direction, and call that copy of $G$ the upper copy. Take a second copy of $G$ that is the reflection of $G$ by $\phi$ , and call that the lower copy. Then we connect the corresponding vertices of the two copies of $G$ by edges that are perpendicular to $S$ , which we call vertical edges. This yields an embedding of $G^{\prime}$ in $M$ such that $(M,G^{\prime},\mathbf{S}^{\prime})$ is a reflection graph.

It remains to show that $(M,G^{\prime},\mathbf{S}^{\prime})$ is a tangle reflection graph. Let $L^{\prime}$ be a link formed from $(G^{\prime},\mathbf{S}^{\prime})$ , with tangles $\mathcal{T}_{1},\dots\mathcal{T}_{2n}$ in the upper copy of $G$ and tangles $\mathcal{T}_{2n+1},\dots,\mathcal{T}_{4n}$ in the lower copy of $G$ .

We form two new links $L^{\prime\prime}$ and $L^{\prime\prime\prime}$ from $(G^{\prime},\mathbf{S}^{\prime})$ such that the first consists of $\mathcal{T}_{1},\dots\mathcal{T}_{2n}$ in the upper copy of $G$ , and then their reflections across the vertical edges in the lower copy of $G$ . The second consists of $\mathcal{T}_{2n+1},\dots,\mathcal{T}_{4n}$ in the lower copy of $G$ and then their reflections across the vertical edges in the upper copy of $G$ . Treating each pair of tangles along a vertical edge as a single tangle, we know that because $(G,\mathbf{S})$ is a tangle reflection graph, we can form the $G$ -replicants of each of the now $2n$ tangles in $L^{\prime\prime}$ and then by cutting along totally geodesic surfaces and regluing, we can create $2n$ copies of $L^{\prime\prime}$ in $M$ . Similarly, from the $2n$ -replicants of the tangles in $L^{\prime\prime\prime}$ we can create $2n$ copies of $L^{\prime\prime\prime}$ in $M$ . In each case, the sum of the volumes of the $2n$ copies of the complements of the links have volumes at least as great as the sum of the volumes of the $G$ -replicants. But each of these links has a reflection surface such that reflecting across it switches the two copies of each $\mathcal{T}_{i}$ within it. So we can cut the manifolds open along the totally geodesic surfaces and reglue to obtain $4n$ copies of $L$ in $M$ . Hence the theorem follows. ∎

The following examples are immediate from the theorem. Our discussion of bracelet links showed that a cycle graph $C_{2n}$ with $2n$ vertices is a tangle reflection graph in $S^{3}$ . That graph can be isotoped to live on a sphere $S$ that is the fixed-point set for a reflection symmetry of the 3-sphere. Therefore Theorem 7.1 implies that we obtain a prism graph with $4n$ vertices that is a tangle reflection graph. Note that each vertex in the graph is trivalent so our tangles have three bundles of strands exiting. We can reapply Theorem 7.1 to the prism graph, since it also can be isotoped to live on a sphere. Thus, we generate a hyperprism graph of $8n$ vertices, as in Figure 19, which must also be a tangle reflection graph. Of course, this last example is also a $(2n,4)$ -torus lattice graph, so we already knew that it was a tangle reflection graph.

*Figure 19. That the cycle graph is a tangle reflection graph in $S^{3}$ implies the prism graph is also, which implies the hyperprism graph is as well.*

Unlike what happened with the cycle graph, in these graphs, we can have any positive number of strands running along an edge, including a single strand.

Another example is generated by the $(2m,2n)$ -torus lattice graph, denoted $G$ , which we know to be a tangle reflection graph. If we take that graph to lie in either the intermediate torus in $T\times(0,1)$ or to lie in the torus splitting $S^{2}\times S^{1}$ into two solid tori, then there is a reflection of the manifold that preserves the torus and therefore the graph. Hence, Theorem 7.1 implies that the graph obtained as a product of $G$ with $P_{1}$ is also a tangle reflection graph in those manifolds.

As further potential tangle reflection graphs, we can look to the 1-skeleta of the Archimedean solids. Three of these solids are relevant to this construction since the only cycles in the 1-skeleta have even length, namely the truncated octahedron, truncated cuboctahedron, and truncated icosidodecahedron.

We observe that in $S^{3}$ , the graphs determined by the $1$ -skeleta of these three solids are reflection graphs. We expect that volume bounds similar to those proven for simpler configurations would hold for links in $S^{3}$ with tangles at the vertices of these Archimedean solids, and connecting strands along the edges. However, the combinatorics quickly becomes difficult.

But note that if these can be shown to be tangle reflection graphs, then Theorem 7.1 implies that their products with $P_{1}$ would also be tangle reflection graphs.

# On the properties of the linear conjugate gradient method

**Authors:** Zexian Liu Qiao Li Affiliation: School of Mathematics and Statistics, Guizhou University, Guiyang, 550025, China

## Abstract

The linear conjugate gradient method is an efficient iterative method for the convex quadratic minimization problems $\mathop{\min}\limits_{x\in{\mathbb{R}^{n}}}f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}x^{T}Ax+b^{T}x$ , where $A\in R^{n\times n}$ is symmetric and positive definite and $b\in R^{n}$ . It is generally agreed that the gradients $g_{k}$ are not conjugate with respective to $A$ in the linear conjugate gradient method (see page 111 in Numerical optimization (2nd, Springer, 2006) by Nocedal and Wright). In the paper we prove the conjugacy of the gradients $g_{k}$ generated by the linear conjugate gradient method, namely,

In addition,a new way is exploited to derive the linear conjugate gradient method based on the conjugacy of the search directions and the orthogonality of the gradients, rather than the conjugacy of the search directions and the exact stepsize.

#### Keywords:

#### MSC

## 1 Introduction

We consider the following convex quadratic optimization problem:

$$ \mathop{\min}\limits_{x\in{R^{n}}}f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}x^{T}Ax+b^{T}x, $$

where $A\in R^{n\times n}$ is symmetric and positive definite and $b\in R^{n}$ .

The linear conjugate gradient method for solving (1.1) has the following form

$$ \begin{array}[]{l}{{x_{k+1}}={x_{k}}+\alpha{{}_{k}}{d_{k}}},\end{array} $$

where $d_{k}$ is the search direction given by

$$ {d_{k}}=\left\{{\begin{array}[]{*{20}{c}}{-{g_{0}},\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;{\rm{if}}\;k=0,}\\
{-{g_{k}}+{\beta_{k}}{d_{k-1}},\;\;\;{\rm{if}}\;k>0,}\end{array}}\right. $$

and $\alpha_{k}$ is the stepsize determined by the exact line search, namely,

$$ {\alpha_{k}}=-\dfrac{g_{k}^{T}d_{k}}{d_{k}^{T}Ad_{k}}=\arg\mathop{\min}\limits_{\alpha>0}f\left({{x_{k}}+\alpha{d_{k}}}\right). $$

It follows from (1.4) that

$$ g_{k+1}^{T}d_{k}=0. $$

Here the parameter $\beta_{k}$ is often derived by making it satisfy the following condition:

$$ d_{k+1}^{T}Ad_{k}=0, $$

which together with (1.5) can yield the conjugacy of the whole search directions, as well as the global convergence. Some well-known formulae for $\beta_{k}$ are called the Fletcher-Reeves (FR) [5], Hestenes-Stiefel (HS) [6], Polak-Ribière-Polyak (PRP) [8, 7] and Dai-Yuan (DY) [4] formulae, and are given by

$$ \beta_{k}^{FR}=\frac{{{{\left\|{{g_{k}}}\right\|}^{2}}}}{{{{\left\|{{g_{k-1}}}\right\|}^{2}}}},\;\;\;\;\beta_{k}^{HS}=\frac{{g_{k}^{T}{y_{k-1}}}}{{d_{k-1}^{T}{y_{k-1}}}},\;\;\;\beta_{k}^{PRP}=\frac{{g_{k}^{T}{y_{k-1}}}}{{{{\left\|{{g_{k-1}}}\right\|}^{2}}}},\;\;\;\beta_{k}^{DY}=\frac{{{{\left\|{{g_{k}}}\right\|}^{2}}}}{{d_{k-1}^{T}{y_{k-1}}}}, $$

where $y_{k-1}=g_{k}-g_{k-1}$ , and $\left\|\cdot\right\|$ denotes the Euclidean norm. In the case that $f$ is given by (1.1) and the exact line search (1.4) is performed, all $\beta_{k}$ should be the same.

It is well-known that the linear conjugate gradient method enjoys the following nice properties.

#### Theorem 1.1

[1, 2] Suppose that the iterate $\left\{x_{k}\right\}$ is generated by the linear conjugate gradient method for solving (1.1), and $x_{k}$ is not the solution point $x^{*}$ . Then,

$$ \begin{array}[]{l}g_{i}^{T}{d_{i}}=-{\left\|{{g_{i}}}\right\|^{2}},\;\;i=0,1,2,\cdots,\\
d_{i}^{T}A{d_{j}}=0,\;\;j=0,1,2,\cdots,i-1,\\
g_{i}^{T}{d_{j}}=0,\;\;j=0,1,2,\cdots,i-1,\\
g_{i}^{T}{g_{j}}=0,\;\;j=0,1,2,\cdots,i-1.\end{array} $$

Further, the sequence $\left\{x_{k}\right\}$ converges to $x^{*}$ in at most $n$ steps.

It follows from Theorem 1.1 that the gradients $g_{k}$ are mutually orthogonal in the linear conjugate gradient method. However, it is generally agreed that the gradients $g_{k}$ generated by the linear conjugate gradient method are not conjugate with respective to $A$ . For example, one can find the well-known description “Since the gradients $r_{k}$ are mutually orthogonal, the term “conjugate gradient method” is actually a misnomer. It is the search directions, not the gradients, that are conjugate with respect to A. ” in Page 111 of Nocedal and Wright’s monograph [3]. Must the gradients generated by the linear conjugate gradient method not be conjugate with respective to the matrix $A$ ? In the paper we will give a negative answer to this question, as well as exploiting a new way for deriving the linear conjugate gradient method based on the conjugacy of the search direction and the orthogonality of the gradient, rather than the conjugacy of the search direction and the exact stepsize.

## 2 The conjugacy of the gradients

In the section we will establish the conjugacy of the gradients generated by the linear conjugate gradient method.

#### Theorem 2.1

Suppose that $\left\{x_{k}\right\}\;\text{and}\;\left\{g_{k}\right\}$ are generated by linear conjugate gradient method for solving (1.1). Then,

$$ \begin{array}[]{l}g_{k+1}^{T}A{g_{k}}=-\dfrac{{\left\|{{g_{k+1}}}\right\|_{2}^{2}}}{{{\alpha_{k}}}}\ ,\\
g_{k+1}^{T}A{g_{i}}=0,\;i=0,1,\cdots,k-1.\end{array} $$

#### Proof

We first prove the first equality in (2.1). If $k=0$ , then it follows from (1.3) and Theorem 1.1 that

$$ g_{1}^{T}A{g_{0}}=-g_{1}^{T}A{d_{0}}=-\frac{1}{{{\alpha_{0}}}}g_{1}^{T}\left({{g_{1}}-{g_{0}}}\right)=-\frac{{\left\|g_{1}\right\|^{2}}}{{{\alpha_{0}}}}. $$

When $k>0$ , we also obtain from the orthogonality of gradients and (1.3) that

$$ \displaystyle g_{k+1}^{T}A{g_{k}} \displaystyle=g_{k+1}^{T}A(-{d_{k}}+\beta{{}_{k}}{d_{k-1}}) \displaystyle=-\frac{{g_{k+1}^{T}({g_{k+1}}-{g_{k}})}}{{\alpha{{}_{k}}}}+\frac{{\beta{{}_{k}}g_{k+1}^{T}({g_{k}}-{g_{k-1}})}}{{\alpha{{}_{k-1}}}} \displaystyle=-\frac{{\left\|{{g_{k+1}}}\right\|_{2}^{2}}}{{{\alpha_{k}}}}. $$

We then prove the second equality in (2.1). If $k=1$ , by (1.3) and Theorem 1.1, we obtain

$$ g_{2}^{T}A{g_{0}}=-g_{2}^{T}A{d_{0}}=-\frac{1}{{{\alpha_{0}}}}g_{2}^{T}\left({{g_{1}}-{g_{0}}}\right)=0. $$

When $k>1$ , it follows from (1.3) and Theorem 1.1 that

$$ \displaystyle g_{k+1}^{T}A{g_{i}} \displaystyle=g_{k+1}^{T}A(-{d_{i}}+\beta{{}_{i}}{d_{i-1}}) \displaystyle=-\frac{{g_{k+1}^{T}({g_{i+1}}-{g_{i}})}}{{\alpha{{}_{i}}}}+\frac{{\beta{{}_{i}}g_{k+1}^{T}({g_{i}}-{g_{i-1}})}}{{\alpha{{}_{i-1}}}} \displaystyle=0, $$

where $\;i=0,1,\cdots,k-1.$ It completes the proof. $\hfill{}\Box$

Remark 1. It follows from Theorem 2.1 that $g_{k+1}$ is conjugate to $g_{i}\;(i=0,1,\cdots,k-1)$ with respective to $A$ . Due to the conjugacy of the gradients, it seems that it is also reasonable to name the iterative method (1.2) and (1.3) with (1.4) the linear conjugate gradient method.

## 3 New way for deriving the linear conjugate gradient method

In the section, we will exploit a new way for deriving the linear conjugate gradient method.

The orthogonality of gradients is crucial to the linear conjugate gradient method. Different from the stepsize (1.4) which makes $f$ reduce mostly along the search direction $d_{k}$ , the new stepsize $\alpha_{k}$ in (1.3) is choose such that the resulting new gradient $g_{k+1}$ is orthogonal to the latest gradient $g_{k}$ , namely,

$$ g_{k+1}^{T}g_{k}=0, $$

which implies that

$$ \alpha_{k}=-\dfrac{g_{k}^{T}g_{k}}{g_{k}^{T}Ad_{k}}. $$

Therefore, the new iterative method has the form (1.2) and (1.3) with (3.2), which is derived based on the conditions:

$$ g_{k+1}^{T}g_{k}=0\;\;\text{and}\;d_{k+1}^{T}Ad_{k}=0.\; $$

Note that it is different from the conditions (1.5) and (1.6) used to derive the linear conjugate gradient method.

In the following theorem, we will prove the equivalence of the iterative method (1.2) and (1.3) with (3.2) and the linear conjugate gradient method.

#### Theorem 3.1

The new stepsize (3.2) is also the exact stepsize, namely, ${\alpha_{k}}=\arg\mathop{\min}\limits_{\alpha>0}f\left({{x_{k}}+\alpha{d_{k}}}\right).$

#### Proof

It follows from $d_{k}^{T}Ad_{k-1}=0$ that $\alpha_{k}=\dfrac{g_{k}^{T}g_{k}}{d_{k}^{T}Ad_{k}}$ . Thus, we have

$$ \begin{array}[]{l}g_{k+1}^{T}{d_{k}}={\left({{g_{k}}+{\alpha_{k}}A{d_{k}}}\right)^{T}}{d_{k}}\\
\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;=g_{k}^{T}{d_{k}}+\frac{{g_{k}^{T}{g_{k}}}}{{d_{k}^{T}A{d_{k}}}}d_{k}^{T}A{d_{k}}\\
\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;={\beta_{k}}g_{k}^{T}{d_{k-1}}\\
\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;={\beta_{k}}{\beta_{k-1}}\cdots{\beta_{1}}g_{1}^{T}{d_{0}}\\
\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;=-{\beta_{k}}{\beta_{k-1}}\cdots{\beta_{1}}g_{1}^{T}{g_{0}}\\
\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;=0,\end{array} $$

which togetcher with (1.1) yields that

$$ {\alpha_{k}}=\arg\mathop{\min}\limits_{\alpha>0}f\left({{x_{k}}+\alpha{d_{k}}}\right). $$

It completes the proof. $\hfill{}\Box$

Remark 2. It follows from Theorem 3.1 that the iterative method (1.2) and (1.3) with (3.2) is indeed the linear conjugate gradient method. Thus we can easily obtain the following corollary.

Remark 3. The above new way for deriving the linear conjugate gradient method might motivate us to design a new criterion that the new trial gradient satisfies, which might make the resulting conjugate gradient method enjoy finite temination property without the exact line search, as well as nice numerical performance.

#### Corollary 1

Suppose that the iterate $\left\{x_{k}\right\}$ is generated by the iterative method (1.2) and (1.3) with (3.2) for solving (1.1), and $x_{k}$ is not the solution point $x^{*}$ . Then, the sequence $\left\{x_{k}\right\}$ converges to $x^{*}$ in at most $n$ steps.

## 4 Conclusion and Discussion

In the paper we establish the conjugacy of the gradients generated by the linear conjugate gradient method, and give a new way for deriving the linear conjugate gradient method based on the orthogonality of the gradients and the conjugacy of the search dirction at the most recent iterations.

However, there are still many questions under investigation. For example, how to design a new design that the new trial gradient satisfies, which might make the resulting conjugate gradient method enjoy nice theoretical property, as well as good numerical performance.
